llm-security.title: COMA: A Compositional Misleading Attack Class on Security-RAG, and a Causal Counterfactual Defense
llm-security.summary: The paper defines COMA, a class of compositional misleading attacks on Security-RAG where each retrieved document is true, instruction-free, non-contradictory, and benign, yet their composition misleads the model. They instantiate COMA via action-corruption (correct diagnosis but inferior remediation) and verdict-flip (exploitability destabilized via undecidable reachability), showing consistent success across five models, two synthetic domains, and a real CVE, with verdict-flip degrading but persisting with stronger models; both succeed when the key disambiguating fact must be inferred rather than read. They introduce CCD, a causal counterfactual defense auditing leave-one-out document influence to flag answers dominated by low-trust sources, localize attacker-controlled docs without false positives on benign controls, and catch influence-spreading adversaries via an aggregate variant, releasing attack seeds and a CCD reference implementation.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It tightens the threat model for security-RAG by showing composition-only attacks that evade standard defenses and offers a causal auditing tool that ML security and foundation model researchers can build on or stress-test.
llm-security.reason: Detecting vulnerability signals in model hidden activations speaks to prefill/internal-state monitoring as a defense against code vulnerabilities and new red-teaming/inspection methods.

llm-security.title: FedLNS: Leverage LayerNorm Signature Modeling to Mitigate Adversarial Manipulation in Federated LLMs
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces FedLNS, a server-side framework that screens federated LLM client updates by modeling changes in trainable normalization-layer parameters as signatures and comparing them to a history-aware cross-client reference. It operates without additional client-to-server metadata, raw client data, trusted server datasets, labeled attack examples, or a separately trained detector, and retains full-model updates for standard or compatible aggregation after screening. Experiments on GPT-, BERT-, and LLaMA-style models trained from scratch with 200 clients show that under 40% target manipulation, FedLNS yields lower test perplexity than six baselines across IID and non-IID partitions.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, data-free, model-internal signal for adversarial update filtering in federated LLM training, aligning with robustness and integrity concerns in LLM security.
llm-security.reason: FedLNS proposes a practical server-side defense against malicious client updates in federated LLM training—directly relevant to attack surfaces (poisoning, integrity) for deployed LLMs.

llm-security.title: Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
llm-security.summary: Auditing step-level credit signals against executed-replay causal ground truth in ALFWorld finds that LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, and policy confidence do not identify causally pivotal steps better than chance, despite performing against annotated correctness. Ground truth contribution is sparse and model-dependent, with substantial variation in counterfactual support across similar-scale policies, and implicit credit tracks policy fluency (high rank correlation) while outcome conditioning adds no causal information. A confidence-only router reduces judge cost modestly without improving pivotal-step detection, and a pre-registered seven-arm training study shows no reliable gains over the base policy, with observed differences attributable to training dose (effective sample size) rather than credit content, implying comparisons must control for dose.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It challenges common step-level credit proxies in agent training and evaluation, highlights the need for causal replay-based auditing, and warns that reported gains may be sample-size artifacts rather than better credit assignment.
llm-security.reason: Direct audit showing step-level credit signals fail to identify causally important agent steps — highly relevant to agent behavior evaluation, red-teaming, and training/credit assignment for tool-using LLM agents.

llm-security.title: MaliciousSkillBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Malicious Agent Skill Detection
llm-security.summary: The authors introduce MaliciousSkillBench, a consolidated benchmark for detecting malicious Agent Skills, normalizing 8,414 raw malicious records into 7,539 unique identities spanning 4,588 structural families and producing a primary set of 9,740 Skills (7,505 malicious, 2,235 benign) after conservative de-duplication and label conflict exclusion. They harmonize 11 attack categories for 4,983 malicious identities and show substantial cross-source threat composition differences. Evaluations of three learned text detectors and three off-the-shelf scanners reveal strong Random/structural-disjoint performance but sharp degradation under Source-Disjoint splits (e.g., TF-IDF SVM 0.932/0.916/0.665 Macro-F1 with 95.6% malicious recall and 62.4% benign FPR on held-out sources), underscoring the need for broader cross-source coverage and joint detection/over-flagging evaluation.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It provides a unified, source-disjoint stress test exposing generalization gaps and FPR trade-offs relevant to LLM agent security and to distribution-shift robustness in foundation models for sequential/structured artifacts.
llm-security.reason: Benchmark consolidating malicious agent Skills addresses a concrete attack surface for agents (malicious skill distribution and detection), directly relevant to LLM security and threat modeling.

llm-security.title: Who Verifies the Benchmark? Decentralizing Trust in Large Language Model Evaluation
llm-security.summary: The paper argues that LLM evaluation lacks verifiability and is vulnerable to unverified vendor claims and LLM-judge identity bias, with real-world consequences highlighted by the January 27, 2025 market panic. Using seven verifier models, it measures how disclosing the source model identity shifts scores across 58 factual, reasoning, political, and preference tasks, finding minimal effects on factual items, moderate effects on stress-reasoning, and large effects on geopolitically sensitive topics, with examples including GLM 5.1 (+7.00, p=0.0249) and Llama 3.3 70B (+1.56, p=0.00). It proposes a blockchain-based commit–reveal protocol with Autonomous Economic Agents to create an on-chain, tamper-evident audit trail that separates blind evaluation from post-hoc claims and eases verification for researchers and leaderboard operators.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to LLM security and evaluation: quantifies identity-aware judge bias across sensitive tasks and offers a verifiable, decentralized commit–reveal protocol that could harden benchmark integrity and leaderboards.
llm-security.reason: Model editing for secure code generation evaluates model-level hardening methods versus inference-time approaches — relevant to reducing malicious or vulnerable generations in deployed LLMs.

llm-security.title: RouteGuard: Certifying Routing Gain in LLM Multi-Agent Systems When Complementarity Is Not Enough
llm-security.summary: The paper shows that common assumptions for multi-agent LLM routing—optimizing gate AUC and relying on advisor complementarity—do not determine deployable gain, and introduces RouteGuard to certify routing benefit. It decomposes gain as G = πΔ_E, identifies a conditional-regret functional Φ as the governing quantity (not AUC), provides a finite-sample certification bracket with a matching Le Cam lower bound that is constant-sharp over the fixed-activity class, and observes a robustness phase transition. Experiments on RouterBench and OpenRCA demonstrate RouteGuard acting as a guardrail, certifying gain only under prompt-level sampling (not workload-cluster resampling) on RouterBench and refusing to certify on OpenRCA due to advisor redundancy, with pre-registered semi-synthetic controls confirming calibration thresholds.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It offers a principled, sample-sensitive certification of routing gain that can prevent illusory improvements in LLM multi-agent systems and aligns evaluation with deployment risk.
llm-security.reason: Analyzes routing certification in LLM multi-advisor systems and provides finite-sample guarantees for when routing yields deployable gain—relevant to safe agent composition, evaluation metrics beyond AUC, and deployment-risk assessment.

llm-security.title: Measure, Don't Optimize: Forecasting Recovery in LLM Unlearning
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces J-Access, an inference-time audit that projects intermediate representations into vocabulary space to measure how often target concepts remain accessible along the output pathway, hypothesizing that residual accessibility predicts recovery susceptibility. Auditing 398 public unlearned models across eight methods, they find most retain accessibility above a retain-only gold level, pre-attack accessibility predicts recovery speed and extent at the model level (but not per-fact), and directly minimizing J-Access causes the model to hide knowledge from the audit while increasing post-attack recovery. They conclude J-Access is useful as a model-level diagnostic for residual susceptibility and caution against turning internal audits into optimization targets without validation.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Offers an actionable, model-level risk signal for unlearning robustness and a clear warning about Goodharting internal audits—relevant for designing secure unlearning and audit pipelines in LLMs.
llm-security.reason: Investigates latent recovery after LLM unlearning with an audit (J‑Access) — important for data‑removal/extraction risk monitoring and evaluation methodology.

llm-security.title: TimeSage-EV: A Live Benchmark for Agentic Time Series Analysis in Evolving Environments
llm-security.summary: TimeSage-EV is a live benchmark for agentic time series analysis that evaluates temporal validity and cutoff-aware evidence use across 60 institutional scenarios and 1,485 scenario-period QA pairs from Feb 2023 to May 2026, spanning multiple release cadences. At each period, LLM agents receive time series data and source reports, with withheld target releases serving as ground truth, and are evaluated on state identification, data summarization, and outlook reasoning. Experiments with frontier LLM agents and TimeSage-1.0, a self-evolving agent with a reusable analytical skill library, show substantial performance gaps and recurring failures in temporal validity, exogenous context use, and adaptation, with monthly updates, code, a leaderboard, and failure-mode analyses released.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It offers a continuously updating, real-world benchmark to stress-test LLM agents’ temporal grounding and adaptability—key for secure, cutoff-aware forecasting and decision support in evolving time series contexts.
llm-security.reason: Analysis of when agent skills fail informs robustness and harness design for agentic systems and red-teaming; valuable for understanding failure modes though somewhat broad.

llm-security.title: DSPrompt: Dynamic Soft Prompt Defense Against M-RAG Corruption
llm-security.summary: DSPrompt defends M-RAG by inserting a few learnable soft prompts into each layer of frozen visual/text encoders, using a shallow-to-deep length schedule to reshape embedding semantics without altering the retrieval pipeline. It trains these prompts via a dynamic min-max scheme with an online multimodal attacker that crafts hard adversarial documents, while the defender pushes them out of top-k and preserves benign ranking/diversity; the defended encoder can be precomputed and indexed like standard dense retrieval with <1% extra parameters and no per-query overhead. Experiments on four benchmarks and three poisoning attacks show substantial reductions in attack success and poison retrieval rates with near-lossless retrieval utility and generation fidelity, outperforming baselines at lower computational cost.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Offers a low-overhead, precomputable defense that hardens retrievers against embedding-space poisoning without query-time detectors—relevant for securing M-RAG and retrieval backbones in LLM pipelines.
llm-security.reason: Defense against embedding-space poisoning for multimodal RAG is directly relevant to retrieval attacks, poisoning defenses, and practical guardrail design.

llm-security.title: Stopping and Routing LLM Judge Panels
llm-security.summary: The work frames judge-panel design as a role-conditioned allocation problem that, using a small labeled audit set, declared slices, and judge costs, estimates target-relative roles: copies, complements, and specialists. These roles yield a policy to drop copies, add complements globally, route specialists on slices, and stop when validation gain falls below a threshold, producing a reusable, auditable call plan. It is empirically compared across multiple audit settings against single judges, flat panels, diversity heuristics, full-call stacking, reliability juries, and frugal cascades, yielding a regime map for when to route specialists, stop in saturated regimes, keep broad ensembles, and ignore conditional copies.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete, auditable routing/early-stopping policy for multi-judge LLM evaluation that balances risk and cost across slices—directly relevant to secure deployment and panel design in LLM oversight and verifiers for time-series or reasoning tasks.
llm-security.reason: Optimizing which judges to call and when directly impacts scalable red-teaming, evaluation budgets, and LLM-as-judge pipelines relevant to security and agent verification.

llm-security.title: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization where an LLM optimizer iteratively edits a target agent’s harness under expensive, stochastic evaluation with a fixed budget, using only graded feedback and without access to a held-out test partition. A trusted execution environment enforces evaluation boundaries, meters resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit, and performance is measured by normalized gain over the seed harness. Evaluating five frontier LLMs across four tasks and 111 runs, the authors find optimizer models differentiate more than coding harnesses, native harnesses aren’t consistently superior, and gains vary substantially by task and seed regime, establishing harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with room for improvement.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It provides a rigorous, auditable setup to compare LLMs’ agentic self-improvement under realistic noisy/expensive evals—relevant for secure agent orchestration and optimizing time-series/tool-using pipelines.
llm-security.reason: Benchmark for optimizing agent harnesses is directly relevant to LLM agent security (attack surface via prompts/tools/orchestration) and offers an evaluation protocol useful for red-teaming and robust harness design.

llm-security.title: Trident : How to Break Deep Reinforcement Learning Cyber Defenses (Agentic)
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces Trident, an agentic LLM red-teaming framework for evaluating DRL-based cyber defenses, consisting of a dynamic benchmark across CybORG CAGE 4 and CyberWheel, a dataset of 13k+ red-blue trajectories for RLVR, and a Code-as-Policy RLVR architecture. Trident reframes red-agent training as a contextual bandit using a Log Summarizer–Planner–Coder pipeline, where a trainable Planner produces complete attack strategies from compressed logs and a frozen Coder turns them into executable Python policies against live DRL defenders. Empirically, a single 7B planner substantially degrades blue-agent performance (average 522% reduction vs. static red baselines) and uncovers emergent behaviors like decoy avoidance and adaptive state prioritization that static heuristics miss.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It demonstrates an RLVR-driven, code-generating agent that reliably breaks DRL cyber defenses and provides a benchmark/dataset, directly informing LLM security evaluation and agent robustness research.
llm-security.reason: Provides trajectory-level certification methods for modular LLM-based security agents, addressing guarantees and calibration across multi-stage pipelines — useful for safety evaluation of agentic security systems.

llm-security.title: Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies closed-form amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase alignment to retrieved past–future windows before feeding them to a frozen TSFM. On a frozen Chronos-Bolt, it outperforms a state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter across seven benchmark datasets (average −3.75% MSE), and it also improves zero-shot MSE by 2.5%–13.7% on four additional frozen TSFMs without per-backbone tuning. Analysis shows aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts in frozen backbones that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out futures-averaging, suggesting frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It challenges the need for learned fusion in RAG for forecasting by showing closed-form alignment on frozen backbones yields SOTA gains and ridge-like in-context adaptation, a strong baseline relevant to LLM alignment and retrieval studies.
llm-security.reason: DASH improves on-policy self-distillation for reasoning models with temporally-adaptive supervision horizons — relevant to improving RL-style fine-tuning and evaluation of reasoning/judging behavior and scalable red-teaming.

llm-security.title: FutureBridge: Token Selection Beyond Local Preference in Collaborative Decoding
llm-security.summary: FutureBridge proposes a token reranking scheme for LLM–SLM collaborative decoding that prioritizes tokens enabling the SLM’s subsequent reasoning rather than the LLM’s local preference. Training uses an answer-verified LLM trajectory to fix a shared future, while a frozen SLM assigns counterfactual scores to candidate tokens under this common context to supervise a lightweight reranker observing only the current state and token. At inference, the LLM only expands the candidate pool and the reranker selects a single token before handing generation back to the SLM without appending any future suffix, yielding a 35.1% relative Math Avg. improvement for Qwen3-1.7B across five math reasoning benchmarks over greedy decoding.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It reframes collaboration as SLM-aware token selection, offering a practical path to safer, stronger small-model reasoning with minimal LLM involvement—relevant to alignment, tool-use gating, and cost/security tradeoffs in cooperative decoding.
llm-security.reason: FutureBridge proposes collaborative decoding between LLM and smaller models to improve SLM reasoning—relevant for efficient red-teaming, agent pipelines, and attack/defense strategies where token choice affects downstream agent behavior.

llm-security.title: Diversity Matters: Distributional Feature Coverage Sample Selection for Data-Efficient Backdoor Attacks
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces DFCS, a training-free, trigger-agnostic sample selection method that clusters pretrained features into one region per poisoning slot and picks centroid-nearest samples to avoid redundant poisons. A local first-order analysis links this allocation to feature-coverage and representative-mass terms. On CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and Imagenette with BadNets and Blended attacks, DFCS achieves the highest mean ASR among seven selectors in all six settings, averaging 96.30% and surpassing the strongest comparator by 4.60 points on average while maintaining clean accuracy.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It highlights a simple, training-free selection principle that boosts low-budget dirty-label backdoor potency, informing both attack design and defenses that rely on data diversity and feature coverage.
llm-security.reason: Data-efficient backdoor attack selection is directly relevant to poisoning threats against models and informs attack surface/defense design, though not LLM-specific and focused on vision-style feature clustering.

llm-security.title: A Four-Axis Trustworthiness Benchmark for LLM-as-Judge in Principle-Based Regulation
llm-security.summary: The paper argues LLM-as-judge for principle-based regulation must be evaluated on four axes: accuracy, paraphrase robustness, adversarial robustness, and calibration, and releases Principle-Bench with 168 FCA-aligned crypto promotion scenarios including paraphrase, keyword-stuffing, and boundary perturbations. It introduces Ceca, a calibrated, auditable assessor emitting per-exemplar counterfactual attributions, and evaluates keyword counting, three sentence-transformer embedders, an open-weight LLM-judge, and a calibrated cascade. Results show no method dominates all axes; a strong 120B judge drops from 0.74 to 0.27 accuracy under keyword-stuffed Consumer Duty inputs and another family’s judge agrees at κ=0.16 on that split, underscoring model-specific failures and the need for per-principle adversarial deception reporting and post-hoc calibration alongside aggregate accuracy.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Offers a concrete, multi-axis benchmark and calibrated assessment method to stress-test LLM judges against paraphrase and adversarial distribution shifts—directly relevant to eval robustness and model governance in safety-critical LLM deployments.
llm-security.reason: LLM-as-judge reliability and adversarial robustness directly relevant to evaluation methodology and guardrail assessment; crypto-financial focus slightly less aligned with core security/time-series interests.

llm-security.title: AccretionLink: On-Device Auditing of Exposure-Control Attacks on Attribute Inference
llm-security.summary: AccretionLink formalizes exposure-control attacks on attribute inference via confidentiality and integrity games, models bounded selection odds with partial identification, and builds dependence-aware time-uniform e-processes. Experiments show odds-four selection improves aggregate negative log likelihood on 52 synthetic profiles at all horizons (e.g., 0.01595 nats at eight posts with 95% CI [0.00890, 0.02336]), with three of four target effects surviving Holm and 6/109 high-confidence false reversals under label-blind model-guided selection; on PAN15, exploratory selection yields a 0.01227-nat advantage without reversals. A TF-IDF selector preserves a 0.01470-nat advantage against an unchanged G5 target not replicated by matched identity shuffling, and on-device auditing on a Pixel 10 uses Tensor G5 with P-256 signing and StrongBox-backed KeyInfo to authenticate digests for selected-replay, actual-model, native-report, and operations.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Offers a concrete, on-device auditing framework and time-uniform testing toolkit for selection-based leakage that parallels concerns in LLM exposure attacks and adaptive evaluation of time-series foundation models.
llm-security.reason: On-device exposure-control attacks for attribute inference are a targeted privacy/adversarial threat relevant to LLM security and data-extraction risk, though focused on user-post ranking rather than LLM-specific tool use.

llm-security.title: Learning What to Fail On: Failure-Mode Contextual Bandits for Adversarial Data Curation
llm-security.summary: The paper frames adversarial data curation as a failure-mode contextual bandit: RAG generates candidates, the target model filters them, an LLM judge ensemble validates them, and clustering groups recurring failure modes. A stochastic policy samples failure modes for retraining using a validation-based reward that trades off robustness gains, forgetting, and data cost, yielding consistent gains over prior adversarial augmentation on SNLI, ANLI, MultiNLI, and transfer to FEVER with RoBERTa variants. They also provide a theoretical interpretation that failure-mode sampling reduces shortcut-aligned gradient contributions while bounding distributional drift, enabling scalable robustness improvements without human annotation.
llm-security.why_it_matters: It operationalizes adaptive, failure-driven data selection with bandit control and LLM-judged RAG—useful for red-teaming LLMs and for principled, cost-aware adversarial curation relevant to secure training and time-series-style foundation data pipelines.
llm-security.reason: Adversarial data curation via failure-mode contextual bandits targets robustness of NLU models and retrieval-augmented synthetic-data pipelines—highly relevant to scalable red-teaming and adversarial training for LLMs.

llm-security.title: Learning the Pareto Frontier of Predictive Models under Distribution Shift
llm-security.summary: The paper introduces Frontier Learning, which treats a library of pretrained models with mixed access regimes (black-box predictions and white-box representations) as complementary sources under distribution shift. It builds a unified target-domain feature by concatenating internal representations from white-box models with outputs from black-box models, then trains a lightweight regularized supervised learner, guaranteeing training-sample risk no worse than any single baseline including zero-shot reuse, fine-tuning, or direct training. Experiments on simulations and real-world shifts (DomainNet/VisDA and MIMIC-IV-Notes ICU mortality) show it matches or outperforms the strongest individual reuse strategy, with the largest gains when no single baseline is reliable across the shifts considered.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Provides a simple, access-agnostic ensemble-on-representations approach that subsumes common reuse strategies and is empirically strong under shift—relevant to robustness/security and modular reuse of foundation models.
llm-security.reason: Agentic BO using LLMs to inject priors into optimization touches on agentic systems and leveraging LLMs as components—relevant to attack/defense surfaces and efficient automated red-teaming workflows.

llm-security.title: Ventor-QTest: Threat-Model-Driven Verification of Vendor-Hosted LLM APIs
llm-security.summary: The paper formalizes hosted model routing as a stochastic process and introduces Ventor-QTest, a black-box audit requiring no probability outputs, with two components: repeated-request estimating average fidelity loss (AFL) via a null-bias-corrected within-window coarsened-KL, and long-sequence estimating extreme fidelity loss (EFL) from the empirical upper tail of a reference-centered-surprisal statistic. AFL shows strong linear agreement with a logprob-based coarsened-KL comparator across three logprob-capable routing conditions, and 20-run sequence probes across seven route snapshots reveal route-specific EFL variation. AFL/EFL exhibit little association with GPQA-Diamond accuracy, but pronounced EFL aligns with reduced Terminal-Bench pass rates under task exposure, motivating joint reporting when auditing long-horizon agentic tasks; code is open-sourced at the provided link.
llm-security.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, probability-free audit to quantify both average and tail fidelity degradation in vendor-hosted LLM routing, directly relevant to red-teaming and reliability of long-horizon agentic deployments.
llm-security.reason: Automated vulnerability detection for AI-generated code touches downstream security risks from LLM outputs, useful but more software-security centric than core LLM attack/defense research.

adversarial-ml.title: Foundation Agents Meet Agentic Deep Research: Evidence-Grounded Clinical Code Forecasting
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper tackles prospective multi-label next-encounter ICD forecasting by composing structured EHR and language foundation models with medical search and ICD dictionaries in a DeepResearch workflow called ICD-Deepresearch. It uses SparseEHR to create an EHR Prior for bounded research expansion, integrates an independent GPT-5 Direct Forecast for complementary candidates, and performs final validation/dedup/ranking with separate rationale generation that doesn’t alter predictions. On MIMIC-III/IV it reports patient-averaged precision/recall of 24.60/35.09% and 25.14/48.32%, and physicians rate its retrieved documents more useful than standalone GPT-5 web search and Medical Deep Research, with improvements over registered local comparators.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Demonstrates an agentic, evidence-grounded composition of EHR and LLM predictors that yields measurable gains in future-code forecasting and retrieval usefulness—relevant to secure, auditable multi-agent workflows for clinical time-series forecasting.
adversarial-ml.reason: COMA describes subtle RAG attacks where benign, factual docs mislead security copilots — highly relevant to RAG poisoning, red-teaming, and security copilots.

adversarial-ml.title: Enhancing Anomaly Resilience in Research Networks: A Large-Scale Forecasting Benchmark for Dynamic Security Baselining
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper introduces a high-fidelity traffic forecasting framework to create dynamic security baselines for RENs, addressing the challenge that elephant flows resemble volumetric attacks to conventional monitors. Using a 57-day Internet2 dataset (13.7B packets across ten backbone routers), it benchmarks six forecasting model families, including SARIMA and long-sequence architectures (TiDE, PatchTST), over 960 configurations. Results show advanced models—especially TiDE—reduce baseline prediction error by 30–42% (p < 0.001) and that a new anomaly-integration strategy yields a 3.3% robustness gain under noise, improving separation of scientific bursts from anomalies.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: It provides a statistically validated, large-scale benchmark showing long-sequence LLM-adjacent forecasters (e.g., TiDE/PatchTST) materially improve dynamic baselining for REN security, informing robust anomaly detection under bursty traffic.
adversarial-ml.reason: AMS detects safety-training modifications via activation geometry across major model families—highly pertinent to model integrity, detection of fine-tune/backdoor changes and LLM security for deployed models.

adversarial-ml.title: When Do PEFT Adaptations Leak Structure? Measuring Black-Box Structural Bounds in Public-Base Model Services
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper introduces VectorHijack-SR, a black-box measurement method that turns paired victim/base residuals into calibrated bounds over PEFT family, layer locality, and coarse rank, using aggregated query-level statistics and a service-disjoint classifier plus a cross-fitted hierarchical rejector to test LoRA-manifold membership. Empirically, family leakage exceeds chance across multiple backbones/tasks, rank inference varies by task, the rejector attains AUROC 0.804 and high known-set accuracy but struggles with structurally close DoRA/LoRA+head, and exact-version linkage on held-out LoRA-r64 services reaches AUC 0.940. Despite measurable structural leakage, experiments show a visibility–exploitability gap: two-stage recovery offers no fair-budget query savings, posterior-selected PEFT underperforms distill-then-convert PEFT, and free-running generation remains near chance.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: It provides concrete, black-box evidence and metrics for structural leakage from PEFTed services with known bases, informing red-team audits, model fingerprinting, and security evaluations of adapter deployment choices.
adversarial-ml.reason: Directly studies information leakage from PEFT adapters in public-base services — highly relevant to model extraction, PIi leakage, and red-team measurement for LLM security.

adversarial-ml.title: Towards a Risk Assessment of Malicious Skill Files in Coding Agents
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper studies the attack surface introduced by agent skill folders in autonomous coding agents and presents an adversarial skill-synthesis method that converts 471 real shell commands into 2,826 benign-looking skills mapped to 11 ATT&CK tactics using six LLMs. It introduces a reproducible evaluation pipeline with stratification, evidence anchoring, refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override, using a three-judge LLM panel validated against a blind human gold standard (κ=0.85). In large-scale tests (5,629 runs), Gemini CLI was exploited in 95.5–96.1% and Qwen Code in 71.6–74.0% of runs with only 1.99% explicit safety recognition, and code/dataset are released at https://github.com/awsm-research/AgentJailbreak.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Provides a validated benchmark, eval pipeline, and high-base-rate exploitation evidence for skill-file attacks in coding agents—directly relevant to LLM security evals and agentic deployment risk.
adversarial-ml.reason: Demonstrates pipeline attack surface in coding agents by hiding malicious shell commands in natural-language skill files — directly applicable to agentic-system attack vectors and red-teaming.

adversarial-ml.title: SkillsMetric: Mapping the Detection Boundary of Static Analysis for Malicious Agent Skills
adversarial-ml.summary: This work introduces SkillsMetric, a five-stage static analysis framework that scores LLM agent skills across pattern density, statistical anomaly, dataflow taint, import anomaly, and capability mismatch. Using an adversarial dataset of 2,266 skills covering 16 attack types and the SkillMD-138K corpus, it reports AUC 0.93 and 5-fold CV F1 73.4%±0.5%, with 93% detection for data exfiltration and steganographic payloads. It also exposes blind spots—0% detection for host destruction via common shell commands and 42% for prompt injection—arguing static analysis alone is insufficient and should be paired with semantic review in defense-in-depth.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Directly maps the detection boundary of static analysis for agent skills, highlighting failure modes (e.g., prompt injection, host destruction) that inform red-teaming, hybrid detection pipelines, and security benchmarks for LLM agents.
adversarial-ml.reason: Static analysis scoring of agent 'skills' maps to supply-chain and capability-based attack surfaces for LLM agents and helps red-teaming/defense of tool-augmented systems.

adversarial-ml.title: An Empirical Study of Output-to-Input Loops for Black-Box Backdoor Detection in Fine-Tuned Open-Weight LLMs
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper proposes self-feeding, a black-box test that recursively feeds a model’s outputs back as inputs to drift toward fine-tuning data, enabling backdoor discovery without training data, clean baselines, or trigger knowledge. Evaluated on six open-weight LLMs (3B–15B) with eleven backdoor categories and twenty prompts over up to ten steps, self-feeding detects backdoors in five models with 92.0% pooled precision, while a same-prompt baseline succeeds on only one of 120 prompt-model pairs; some prompts (jokes, arithmetic, coffee recipes) reach triggers in a few steps. Despite low per-prompt recall (19.2%), multi-prompt use raises model-level detection, though one model never triggers and there are two false positives; truncating to four steps preserves 100% model-level precision and cuts queries by 60%.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Offers a cheap, black-box, text-only stress test that surfaces fine-tune data modes (including backdoors) via output-to-input loops, complementing existing evals for open-weight LLMs and informing detection strategies for security-focused and time-series-style iterative generation analyses.
adversarial-ml.reason: Black‑box self‑feeding method for detecting backdoors in fine‑tuned open LLMs is directly applicable to model vetting, backdoor detection, and practical security checks for deployed models.

adversarial-ml.title: Measuring Task-Agnostic Training Data Influence Across Language Model Pretraining
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper introduces a task-agnostic measure of training data influence that quantifies how much an example’s gradient update reduces the squared distance to a run’s final parameters, estimated from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applied to 18 Pythia and PolyPythia configurations, the method reveals systematic temporal shifts in influential data: literature-related data align more with the parameter trajectory early, while STEM data align more later. This qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across configurations, offering a tractable trajectory-level perspective that complements task-based influence analyses.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Gives a practical, retraining-free way to map which data sources steer pretraining trajectories over time, informing data curation, curriculum, and security-relevant provenance audits for LLMs.
adversarial-ml.reason: Proposes a task-agnostic measure of individual-example influence during LM pretraining which is highly relevant to data provenance, extraction/attribution, contamination, and training-time attack/defense analysis.

adversarial-ml.title: The More Popular, The Harder to Forget: Adaptive Popularity for LLM Unlearning
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper observes that popular facts are memorized more deeply in LLM pretraining and are harder to unlearn, while prior unlearning methods apply uniform gradient pressure regardless of frequency. It proposes AdaPop, which scales unlearning pressure using local token confidence and a per-fact popularity-dependent exponent from an external proxy, and uses a dual-ascent controller to automatically tune the retain penalty each epoch. On three model families and two benchmarks, AdaPop reduces leakage of forgotten content by ~5x on paraphrases and ~1.6x on adversarial reformulations, with internal metrics showing larger divergence from pre-unlearning states on the forget set and closer retention on the retain set compared to baselines.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Targets frequency-aware unlearning with automated retain/forget control, improving robustness to paraphrase/adversarial probes—relevant for red-teaming, safety fine-tuning, and deployment-time data governance.
adversarial-ml.reason: Directly tackles unlearning/memorization—a core LLM security concern (data extraction, forgetting) with a practical adaptive method and measured leakage improvements.

adversarial-ml.title: FedLNS: Leverage LayerNorm Signature Modeling to Mitigate Adversarial Manipulation in Federated LLMs
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper introduces FedLNS, a server-side framework that screens federated LLM client updates by modeling changes in trainable normalization-layer parameters as signatures and comparing them to a history-aware cross-client reference. It operates without additional client-to-server metadata, raw client data, trusted server datasets, labeled attack examples, or a separately trained detector, and retains full-model updates for standard or compatible aggregation after screening. Experiments on GPT-, BERT-, and LLaMA-style models trained from scratch with 200 clients show that under 40% target manipulation, FedLNS yields lower test perplexity than six baselines across IID and non-IID partitions.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, data-free, model-internal signal for adversarial update filtering in federated LLM training, aligning with robustness and integrity concerns in LLM security.
adversarial-ml.reason: FedLNS proposes a practical server-side defense against malicious client updates in federated LLM training—directly relevant to attack surfaces (poisoning, integrity) for deployed LLMs.

adversarial-ml.title: MaliciousSkillBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Malicious Agent Skill Detection
adversarial-ml.summary: The authors introduce MaliciousSkillBench, a consolidated benchmark for detecting malicious Agent Skills, normalizing 8,414 raw malicious records into 7,539 unique identities spanning 4,588 structural families and producing a primary set of 9,740 Skills (7,505 malicious, 2,235 benign) after conservative de-duplication and label conflict exclusion. They harmonize 11 attack categories for 4,983 malicious identities and show substantial cross-source threat composition differences. Evaluations of three learned text detectors and three off-the-shelf scanners reveal strong Random/structural-disjoint performance but sharp degradation under Source-Disjoint splits (e.g., TF-IDF SVM 0.932/0.916/0.665 Macro-F1 with 95.6% malicious recall and 62.4% benign FPR on held-out sources), underscoring the need for broader cross-source coverage and joint detection/over-flagging evaluation.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: It provides a unified, source-disjoint stress test exposing generalization gaps and FPR trade-offs relevant to LLM agent security and to distribution-shift robustness in foundation models for sequential/structured artifacts.
adversarial-ml.reason: Benchmark consolidating malicious agent Skills addresses a concrete attack surface for agents (malicious skill distribution and detection), directly relevant to LLM security and threat modeling.

adversarial-ml.title: DSPrompt: Dynamic Soft Prompt Defense Against M-RAG Corruption
adversarial-ml.summary: DSPrompt defends M-RAG by inserting a few learnable soft prompts into each layer of frozen visual/text encoders, using a shallow-to-deep length schedule to reshape embedding semantics without altering the retrieval pipeline. It trains these prompts via a dynamic min-max scheme with an online multimodal attacker that crafts hard adversarial documents, while the defender pushes them out of top-k and preserves benign ranking/diversity; the defended encoder can be precomputed and indexed like standard dense retrieval with <1% extra parameters and no per-query overhead. Experiments on four benchmarks and three poisoning attacks show substantial reductions in attack success and poison retrieval rates with near-lossless retrieval utility and generation fidelity, outperforming baselines at lower computational cost.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Offers a low-overhead, precomputable defense that hardens retrievers against embedding-space poisoning without query-time detectors—relevant for securing M-RAG and retrieval backbones in LLM pipelines.
adversarial-ml.reason: Defense against embedding-space poisoning for multimodal RAG is directly relevant to retrieval attacks, poisoning defenses, and practical guardrail design.

adversarial-ml.title: Diversity Matters: Distributional Feature Coverage Sample Selection for Data-Efficient Backdoor Attacks
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper introduces DFCS, a training-free, trigger-agnostic sample selection method that clusters pretrained features into one region per poisoning slot and picks centroid-nearest samples to avoid redundant poisons. A local first-order analysis links this allocation to feature-coverage and representative-mass terms. On CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and Imagenette with BadNets and Blended attacks, DFCS achieves the highest mean ASR among seven selectors in all six settings, averaging 96.30% and surpassing the strongest comparator by 4.60 points on average while maintaining clean accuracy.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: It highlights a simple, training-free selection principle that boosts low-budget dirty-label backdoor potency, informing both attack design and defenses that rely on data diversity and feature coverage.
adversarial-ml.reason: Data-efficient backdoor attack selection is directly relevant to poisoning threats against models and informs attack surface/defense design, though not LLM-specific and focused on vision-style feature clustering.

adversarial-ml.title: ProbGuard: Calibrated Safety Risk Estimation from LLM Output Distributions
adversarial-ml.summary: ProbGuard reframes LLM safety assessment as probabilistic risk estimation over the model’s early output distribution rather than deterministic classification on completed token sequences. It estimates the probability of unsafe continuation via Monte Carlo over generated prefix distributions and calibrates this risk through post-training, enabling early stopping of unsafe generations. Empirically, it achieves the best calibration across nine model–dataset settings (average Brier and ECE reduced by 79.6% and 71.9% vs. the best baseline) and caps jailbreak attack success to ≤1% after only the first ten decoding steps.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: It operationalizes distribution-aware, early-stage safety control with strong calibration—useful for red-teaming defenses, risk-sensitive deployment, and aligning with probabilistic guardrail research and time-series-style forecasting over generation trajectories.
adversarial-ml.reason: Proposes a novel metric (feature nonlocality) to assess abstraction level of learned features from sparse autoencoders; useful for mechanistic interpretability and evaluating claims about high-level features relevant to jailbreak/mechanistic work.

adversarial-ml.title: AccretionLink: On-Device Auditing of Exposure-Control Attacks on Attribute Inference
adversarial-ml.summary: AccretionLink formalizes exposure-control attacks on attribute inference via confidentiality and integrity games, models bounded selection odds with partial identification, and builds dependence-aware time-uniform e-processes. Experiments show odds-four selection improves aggregate negative log likelihood on 52 synthetic profiles at all horizons (e.g., 0.01595 nats at eight posts with 95% CI [0.00890, 0.02336]), with three of four target effects surviving Holm and 6/109 high-confidence false reversals under label-blind model-guided selection; on PAN15, exploratory selection yields a 0.01227-nat advantage without reversals. A TF-IDF selector preserves a 0.01470-nat advantage against an unchanged G5 target not replicated by matched identity shuffling, and on-device auditing on a Pixel 10 uses Tensor G5 with P-256 signing and StrongBox-backed KeyInfo to authenticate digests for selected-replay, actual-model, native-report, and operations.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Offers a concrete, on-device auditing framework and time-uniform testing toolkit for selection-based leakage that parallels concerns in LLM exposure attacks and adaptive evaluation of time-series foundation models.
adversarial-ml.reason: On-device exposure-control attacks for attribute inference are a targeted privacy/adversarial threat relevant to LLM security and data-extraction risk, though focused on user-post ranking rather than LLM-specific tool use.

adversarial-ml.title: Analysis of Federated Aggregation under Model Poisoning and Backdoor Attacks: A Reconstructed Cross-Dataset and Cross-Architecture Benchmark
adversarial-ml.summary: This work reconstructs a 500-cell federated aggregation benchmark across five methods, five datasets, five architectures, and four conditions (clean, sign-flipping, Gaussian, BadNets), recovering 454 original runs and 36 repairs/reruns, with 10 SVHN cells covered only by summary provenance. Trimmed Mean has the best clean macro-mean accuracy and lowest mean within-task rank, while Krum shows the top recorded accuracy under sign-flipping and Gaussian, and these rankings persist when restricted to fully logged task pairs. Audits reveal the BadNets metric is actually TTLR (all test inputs triggered) and a FedPARETO pathway where reported predictive summaries may not match the corrupted updates used for aggregation, so results are descriptive within recorded configs rather than universal robustness claims.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Highlights reproducibility gaps, metric mis-specification (TTLR), and aggregation/provenance pitfalls that can confound robustness claims in federated settings relevant to secure FL and poisoning/backdoor evaluation.
adversarial-ml.reason: Cross‑dataset benchmark for federated aggregation under poisoning/backdoors informs robust evaluation and threat models though it's more federated learning than LLM‑specific.

adversarial-ml.title: Into the ORBIT for Time Series: Training Regimes for Foundation Models
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper introduces ORBIT, a training paradigm for TSFMs that explicitly controls pre-training distributions via Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling and Omni-Range Incremental Training. It trains Falcon-2.0, a univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction, under this regime. The authors also propose Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment to align shallow and deep representations, and report strong zero-shot forecasting on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench across diverse domains and frequencies.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: It provides a principled, controllable pretraining regime and lightweight representation alignment that could transfer to secure LLM pretraining curricula and to robust TSFM deployment across heterogeneous, imbalanced time-series corpora.
adversarial-ml.reason: Evaluation metric for synthetic limit-order-book time series is relevant for TSFM evaluation and assessing generative-model fidelity, with potential security implications for market-simulation attacks.

adversarial-ml.title: Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Generalizable Vulnerability Detection in IoT Firmware
adversarial-ml.summary: The paper introduces IoTVulBench, a human-verified, contamination-screened benchmark for cross-corpus IoT firmware vulnerability detection, and evaluates five model architectures, two tuning methods, and three curriculum strategies with ensemble, distillation, and robustness analyses. Models trained on IoTVulBench outperform matched single-source datasets (MCC 0.58 vs. 0.44 for PrimeVul and 0.39 for D2A), with staged curriculum learning raising MCC to 0.69 and a diversity-optimized ensemble reaching 0.73, surpassing a static analyzer (0.31) and PrimeVul by large margins while maintaining 86% performance under identifier renaming and showing strong calibration and largely faithful explanations. At a 0.5% FPR, the model missed 21% of vulnerabilities versus 71% for the strongest comparator, indicating domain-matched data and curriculum design—not model scale alone—drive generalization in firmware vulnerability detection.
adversarial-ml.why_it_matters: Provides a contamination-screened, human-verified benchmark and concrete training/curriculum/ensemble recipes that substantially improve cross-corpus generalization—useful for LLM security evaluation and for designing data- and curriculum-centric pipelines beyond scaling.
adversarial-ml.reason: IoT firmware vulnerability detection benchmark is relevant to broader adversarial robustness and benchmark validity but outside core LLM/security or time‑series focus.

tsfm.title: Tevatron-Elastic: A Unified Abstraction for Training Elastic Retrievers and Rerankers
tsfm.summary: Tevatron-Elastic introduces a unified abstraction that encapsulates three orthogonal elasticity axes for IR models—fewer layers, upper-layer token pruning, and shorter embeddings—so a single checkpoint supports multiple runtime sizes selected via a schedule. The abstraction applies uniformly to retrievers and rerankers, encoder and decoder backbones via HF interfaces, subsuming prior methods like Matryoshka embeddings, early exit, 2D Matryoshka (e.g., Starbucks), and layerwise token compression, and also enables Matryoshka LTC for jointly training multiple token-compression ratios in one retriever. Empirically, across 20 checkpoints, three backbones, and two tasks, they report smooth quality curves, near-single-size training cost, and controlled wallclock speedups, releasing the framework and checkpoints for elastic retrieval systems.
tsfm.why_it_matters: A clean, composable interface for multi-axis elasticity in retrievers/rerankers simplifies deployment-time cost/quality trade-offs and unifies techniques ML security and systems folks already use (early exit, Matryoshka, token compression) under one training/checkpoint regime.
tsfm.reason: Elastic retrievers/rerankers address scalable retrieval tradeoffs and dynamic model-size/runtime adaptation—useful for efficient RAG/agent pipelines and evaluation of retrieval components in security workflows.

tsfm.title: Intern-S2-Preview: Scientific Agentic Foundation Model
tsfm.summary: Intern-S2-Preview introduces scientific agentic foundation models trained via multimodal pretraining on rendered scientific documents, interleaved image-text, and diverse scientific corpora, followed by a unified post-training stack of SFT, scalable multi-task RL, black- and white-box agentic RL, and on-policy distillation. The pipeline adds practical rollout/training techniques—partial rollout with off-policy correction, adaptive length regularization, online speculative decoding, robust multi-task optimization, and trace-aware experience assembly—and explores architecture-level extensions: a 397B model with time series modules for efficient long-sequence understanding and numerical forecasting, plus a separate Memory Decoder path for rapid specialization without changing the frozen backbone. Evaluations report competitive or leading results across scientific, multimodal, agentic, and general-purpose benchmarks, with time-series gains on SciTS and a MemDec-4B extension improving Biology-Instructions average from 56.92 to 60.32 without modifying the 397B backbone.
tsfm.why_it_matters: Brings a concrete agentic RL + multimodal + TS forecasting stack with stability tricks and a memory-augmented specialization path relevant to secure tool-use agents and time-series LLMs.
tsfm.reason: Agentic multimodal scientific foundation model work intersects with agentic-system attack surfaces and long-horizon reasoning, relevant for security analysis though not focused on adversarial robustness.

tsfm.title: Probing the Prefill: Detecting Code Vulnerabilities via Latent Activations
tsfm.summary: The authors test whether LLM hidden states during prefill encode vulnerability signals when reading C/C++ code by extracting last prefill token activations from four models and training small MLP probes. Across four function-level benchmarks (Devign, Big-Vul, Draper VDISC, PrimeVul), probes (13.4–16.0M params, <0.2% of base) reach 41.7% average F1, with a Qwen3.5-9B probe hitting 68.8% F1 on Devign, comparable to a fine-tuned-classifier SOTA (67.9%). Performance lags SOTA on the more imbalanced datasets, indicating partial but meaningful vulnerability information in frozen, general-purpose LLM activations and motivating model-native screening approaches.
tsfm.why_it_matters: Shows actionable signal for vulnerability detection resides in prefill activations, suggesting low-overhead, model-native monitors as an alternative or complement to post-hoc judges/classifiers.
tsfm.reason: Reproduction and sensitivity analysis of WEASEL 2.0 across UCR datasets is directly relevant to time-series benchmark validity and practical model choices (ensemble sizing).

tsfm.title: SkillTFM: Gated Skill Evolution for Training-Free Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models
tsfm.summary: The paper introduces SkillTFM, a training-free adaptation system for tabular foundation models that replaces parameter updates with gated evolution of agentic skills. It uses a verifiable, extensible skill bank combining boundary evidence identification to characterize task structure and base-model failures with gated skill evolution to retrieve and extend reusable skills under explicit validation. In simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128–0.142, elevating nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898, and shows effectiveness across different TFM backbones.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It proposes a security-adjacent, verifiable skill-gating mechanism for training-free adaptation under distribution shift, echoing modular skill libraries and guarded tool-use in LLMs while targeting tabular/time-series TFMs.
tsfm.reason: Empirical study of self-pretraining for medical time series—useful data on pretraining benefits and transfer in noisy, multimodal TS settings though domain-specific.

tsfm.title: LabelFusion-TS: Fusing Large Language Models, Transformer Encoders, and Financial Time Series for Monetary-Policy Stance Classification
tsfm.summary: The paper introduces LabelFusion-TS, which combines a fine-tuned RoBERTa encoder, a prompted LLM, and an ensemble of time-series transformers over pre-publication market series via a small voting network to classify FOMC sentences as hawkish, dovish, or neutral. Due to limited human labels (~1k sentences), the RoBERTa encoder is first pre-trained on LLM-generated weak labels and then fine-tuned on human annotations. Trained on data up to 2015 and evaluated on 2015–2022, the fused system attains 70.2% weighted F1, surpassing a zero-shot LLM at 64.1% and overtaking it with as few as 240 human-labeled sentences.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It demonstrates measurable gains from fusing market time series with LLM/text encoders for monetary-policy stance classification, highlighting a practical multimodal path beyond text-only classifiers.
tsfm.reason: Multimodal fusion of financial time series with LLMs for stance classification touches the reader's TSFM interest (benchmarks/architectures) and evaluation, though it's a narrow financial NLP application.

tsfm.title: Into the ORBIT for Time Series: Training Regimes for Foundation Models
tsfm.summary: The paper introduces ORBIT, a training paradigm for TSFMs that explicitly controls pre-training distributions via Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling and Omni-Range Incremental Training. It trains Falcon-2.0, a univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction, under this regime. The authors also propose Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment to align shallow and deep representations, and report strong zero-shot forecasting on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench across diverse domains and frequencies.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It provides a principled, controllable pretraining regime and lightweight representation alignment that could transfer to secure LLM pretraining curricula and to robust TSFM deployment across heterogeneous, imbalanced time-series corpora.
tsfm.reason: Evaluation metric for synthetic limit-order-book time series is relevant for TSFM evaluation and assessing generative-model fidelity, with potential security implications for market-simulation attacks.

tsfm.title: Revisiting WEASEL 2.0: Reproduction, Sensitivity, and an Adaptive Ensemble-Size Rule
tsfm.summary: The paper reproduces WEASEL 2.0 on 114 UCR datasets, matching reported accuracy (mean 0.865, median 0.928; Wilcoxon p = 0.655). It probes sensitivity of four design choices, finding the downstream classifier, lack of feature weighting, and the max window-size rule to be robust, while the fixed max ensemble-size rule is over-provisioned for long series. An adaptive rule based on series length and number of classes cuts peak fit memory and time on fixed-length datasets with essentially no median accuracy change.
tsfm.why_it_matters: Offers a principled, resource-saving ensemble-size heuristic for dictionary TSC that preserves accuracy—useful for scaling long-sequence models and benchmarking efficient TS foundations.
tsfm.reason: Reproduction and sensitivity analysis of a time-series classifier (WEASEL 2.0) is directly relevant to TSFM benchmarking and methodological rigor, but it's a classical classifier rather than a foundation-model pretraining advance.

tsfm.title: Feature Priming in Online Linear Regression: Sparse-Regret Lower Bounds and a Tight Univariate Rate
tsfm.summary: The paper studies feature priming for high-dimensional online linear regression and answers a COLT 2023 question negatively for three Moore–Penrose priming rules, showing sparse-logarithmic regret is impossible under a natural past-data protocol. It identifies nuisance interpolation as the mechanism that underweights the predictive coordinate and proves Ω(min{T, sqrt(d)}) regret via Hadamard-style constructions, even against a zero-loss one-sparse comparator, with variants for prime powers and rule selection. On the positive side, it shows regret controlled by data rank and matches this with a Euclidean-normalized triangular lower bound for powered univariate priming (robust to nonnegative ridge), plus a paired ridge construction covering all three powered rules, and reports diagnostics on frozen LM activations reflecting the same failure mode; multivariate and Pearson frontiers remain open.
tsfm.why_it_matters: Clarifies limits of sparsity-seeking online priming and ties them to concrete interpolation pathologies also observed in LM activations, informing robust feature selection and security-relevant guardrails.
tsfm.reason: JEPA/world-model anti-collapse methods and contrastive inverse dynamics propose pretraining objectives relevant to time-series/world-model representation learning, offering alternatives to Gaussian regularizers though not directly TS forecasting.

tsfm.title: Task-Conditioned Least-Privilege Learning for Executable Terminal and MCP Agents
tsfm.summary: The paper introduces a post-training framework to teach a 4B LLM to select task-conditioned authority in executable terminal and MCP settings, complementing permission gates and sandboxing. It uses deterministic verifiers auditing actions pre- and post-execution along six risk dimensions, combined with task-specific sufficient-authority envelopes to compute excess-privilege signals for optimization, and is trained on Qwen3.5-4B over 1,500 tasks. On 500 held-out tasks (2,896 episodes) the trained model achieves 98.48% safe success vs. 64.36% for the base policy and reduces excess-authority errors from 4.56% to 0.79%, with external tests showing capability retention/prompt-directed improvement and a 400-task continuation indicating generalization with a 6.99 pp reduction in excess-authority events.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It proposes and empirically validates a least-privilege post-training signal for tool-use agents, directly addressing excess-authority risks in executable/MCP settings without degrading capabilities.
tsfm.reason: Two-stage distillation of tabular foundation models into lightweight predictors is relevant for efficient deployment of foundation-style models, though focused on tabular rather than time-series.

tsfm.title: Temporal Leakage in Financial News NLP: A Multi-Architecture Audit with a Regime-Specific M&A Signal
tsfm.summary: The paper audits temporal leakage in financial-news direction prediction across 49,799 articles and 16 model–feature setups (TF-IDF, MiniLM, FinBERT, fine-tuned RoBERTa-large/DeBERTa-v3-large, and Llama-3/Qwen2.5 zero/few-shot and LoRA), finding random splits inflate MCC by 1.1×–6.5×, increasing with capacity and feature richness, and that end-to-end FinBERT fine-tuning further amplifies the gap (size-matched ratio 1.75×). Under near-chronological evaluation, only M&A shows a positive locked-test signal (TF-IDF MCC 0.138 train-only, 0.068 after train∪val refit; 10,000-permutation p < 10^{-3}), which does not transfer to FNSPID 2009–2020 U.S. data, suggesting localization to 2024–2025 European-tilted M&A semantics. Three role labelers indicate acquirer-tagged articles as the signal locus, and the authors argue chronological splits purge stale, predictable components, leaving a small, event-localized, lexically shallow residual and call for mandatory leakage audits in financial NLP benchmarks.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It quantifies temporal leakage effects across classic NLP and LLM settings, isolates a regime-specific residual signal, and argues for leakage audits—directly informing robust evaluation protocols for security-relevant LLMs and time-series-oriented foundation models.
tsfm.reason: ICD forecasting and composing foundation models for longitudinal EHR is relevant to time-series foundation models and prospective forecasting, though clinical focus and integration with search reduces immediate relevance to core TSFM methodology.

tsfm.title: No Gaussian Required: Contrastive Inverse Dynamics for JEPA World Models
tsfm.summary: The paper proposes Action-Contrastive Masked Transition Modeling (AC-MTM) for JEPA world models, replacing LeWM’s SIGReg Gaussian latent regularizer with a training-only inverse-dynamics head optimized via Action-NCE to prevent representation collapse. This contrastive inverse branch ensures each latent transition identifies its generating action among batch negatives, is discarded after training, and leaves test-time behavior identical to LeWM. AC-MTM matches SIGReg on four standard pixel-control tasks under a matched planner and substantially outperforms it on OGBench Visual Scene (80.0±2.0% vs 58.0±2.0%), suggesting prescribed latent geometry can bottleneck performance; code is released at the provided GitHub link.
tsfm.why_it_matters: It offers a distribution-free, target-network-free anti-collapse mechanism for JEPA-style world models that scales to harder visual control, directly relevant to secure, robust representation learning without prescriptive latent priors.
tsfm.reason: JEPA world-model work on contrastive inverse dynamics may inform representation objectives useful for time-series or sequential modeling, but it's primarily a world-model / vision-style contribution rather than TSFM security.

agents.title: HarnessSafe: Evaluating Safety Across Persistent Carriers in Agent Harnesses
agents.summary: The paper introduces HarnessSafe, a benchmark of 328 executable cases spanning seven persistent-carrier families to assess delayed safety risks in agent harnesses that persist state across tasks and sessions. Each case is defined as a Persistent-Risk Lifecycle that traces attacker influence from entry through cross-carrier persistence to a benign trigger and an observable violation, and a multi-stage, trace-based evaluation measures how far each attack progresses and where it is stopped. Experiments indicate containment is carrier-specific and depends strongly on the harness-model configuration, with both harness and model shaping outcomes and attack success rates failing to capture lifecycle progression patterns.
agents.why_it_matters: It offers a carrier-aware, trace-based methodology and dataset to dissect how safety risks propagate across memory/tools/skills in agentic systems—complementing coarse success-rate metrics and informing defense design in LLM agents and persistent pipelines.
agents.reason: Benchmarks delayed safety risks from persistent carriers in agent harnesses; directly targets attack surfaces (memory, tools, skills), evaluation methodology, and end-to-end exploit propagation — highly relevant to LLM security and agentic threat models.

agents.title: Toward Metacognitive One-Shot Indirect Prompt Injection: Strategy Abstraction Via Outcome-Conditioned Reflection
agents.summary: The paper introduces SAVOR, a one-shot IPI attack framework that moves adaptation offline via outcome-conditioned reflection over successful and failed trajectories from disjoint training environments, consolidating validated, context-conditioned strategies into a reusable strategy memory. At test time, the frozen memory generates a single payload per unseen target without iterative interaction or feedback, achieving the highest average attack success rate across two benchmarks and three victim models. On Agent Security Bench and the new executable OpenClaw-IPI, SAVOR outperforms the strongest prior attack by 2.5–11.8 points and beats the same injection channel without strategy learning by 23.1 and 28.6 points respectively, with learned memory transferring across defenses.
agents.why_it_matters: Demonstrates practical one-shot IPI via offline strategy distillation that generalizes across tools, goals, and defenses—relevant for red-teaming LLM agents and for designing defenses that hold under realistic single-interaction constraints.
agents.reason: One-shot indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks on tool-using agents via offline strategy distillation directly targets agentic attack surfaces and realistic attacker models—highly relevant to LLM security and red-teaming methodology.

agents.title: From Runnable to Verifiable: An Independent Reproducibility Study of LLM/Agent-Driven Vulnerability Validation Artifacts
agents.summary: This pre-registered reproducibility audit examines LLM/agent-driven vulnerability validation artifacts across 104 papers (2023–2026), finding only 59 with publicly reachable artifacts and executing 18 paper-level workflows and 102 anchor benchmark cases. It reports high mismatch and fragility: 58/102 anchor cases have internal CVE IDs diverging from directory labels; only 10/18 artifacts run end-to-end at R0 (11/18 after R1 env-only fixes); and embedded oracles are unreliable, with 20/30 patched-counterfactuals still signaling and 7/19 negative controls triggering, yielding oracle sensitivity 60% and specificity 45%. The study argues that vulnerable-build triggers are not CVE-specific evidence without a clean patched counterfactual and offers a reusable, pre-registered protocol (post-conditions, R0/R1 repair ladder, G1–G3 evidence levels, patched-counterfactual oracles) for the community.
agents.why_it_matters: It surfaces concrete failure modes and a reusable protocol for verifying LLM/agent security claims—directly informing eval design, oracle construction, and counterfactual controls for both LLM security and time-series-style benchmark reproducibility.
agents.reason: ActBench proposes an execution-trajectory-based behavioral safety benchmark for cowork agents, directly applicable to evaluating agent risks like data leakage and unauthorized actions—highly relevant for tooling and red-teaming.

agents.title: ElasticBack: Stealthy Conditional Backdoor in LLM-Agent Skills via Coupled Trigger-Rule Optimization
agents.summary: The paper introduces ElasticBack, a conditional single-skill backdoor for LLM agents that couples a malicious rule R in the skill document with a benign-looking trigger T in user queries, activating only when both appear. It constructs R via semantic-anchored rule injection and then fixes R while evolving T using a stealth-constrained genetic search to optimize attack effectiveness and stealth without modifying model weights. Experiments over three target behaviors (50 skills each) and four agent LLMs show high ASR with near-zero FPR, preserved clean accuracy, cross-model transfer, and evasion of deployment-time defenses, motivating stronger supply-chain defenses for skills.
agents.why_it_matters: Highlights a practical, weight-free, conditional backdoor vector in the emerging agent skill ecosystem, relevant to securing tool-using LLMs and evaluating defenses against stealthy trigger-rule couplings.
agents.reason: Presents a stealthy conditional backdoor attack targeting agent skills (supply-chain threat) with low-cost single-skill triggers—highly relevant to LLM agent security, tool/skill poisoning, and defense evaluation.

agents.title: On Understanding, Identifying, and Mitigating Vulnerabilities in Agentic Large Language Models
agents.summary: This paper reviews 85 papers (2023–2025) on security of agentic LLMs, selected via a PRISMA 2020 systematic process from 743 records, finding attack work outpaces defenses by 3.9:1. It reports that perception-layer vulnerabilities (prompt injection, jailbreaking, adversarial perturbations) dominate at 66%, while action-layer issues (tool misuse, code injection, sandbox escape) are only 4.7%, with code execution at 3.5% and tool-augmented agents at 12%. The authors propose a four-layer taxonomy (perception, brain, action, interaction) covering 13 vulnerability types, identify seven open problems focused on containment, and argue that weak isolation and architectural coupling let failures propagate across layers.
agents.why_it_matters: It quantifies where current security work is misaligned with real agentic risk surfaces and offers a layered taxonomy and containment-focused agenda that can guide rigorous evaluations and defenses for tool-using, code-executing LLM agents.
agents.reason: Systematic review focused on vulnerabilities unique to agentic LLMs (tool use, persistent memory, state changes) directly matches the reader's primary interest in agent attack surfaces and red‑teaming.

agents.title: Foundation Agents Meet Agentic Deep Research: Evidence-Grounded Clinical Code Forecasting
agents.summary: The paper tackles prospective multi-label next-encounter ICD forecasting by composing structured EHR and language foundation models with medical search and ICD dictionaries in a DeepResearch workflow called ICD-Deepresearch. It uses SparseEHR to create an EHR Prior for bounded research expansion, integrates an independent GPT-5 Direct Forecast for complementary candidates, and performs final validation/dedup/ranking with separate rationale generation that doesn’t alter predictions. On MIMIC-III/IV it reports patient-averaged precision/recall of 24.60/35.09% and 25.14/48.32%, and physicians rate its retrieved documents more useful than standalone GPT-5 web search and Medical Deep Research, with improvements over registered local comparators.
agents.why_it_matters: Demonstrates an agentic, evidence-grounded composition of EHR and LLM predictors that yields measurable gains in future-code forecasting and retrieval usefulness—relevant to secure, auditable multi-agent workflows for clinical time-series forecasting.
agents.reason: COMA describes subtle RAG attacks where benign, factual docs mislead security copilots — highly relevant to RAG poisoning, red-teaming, and security copilots.

agents.title: SCALE: State-Calibrated Latent Embeddings for JEPA Planning in the Right Geometry
agents.summary: The paper studies JEPA-style planning where terminal embedding costs depend on representation geometry, comparing DINO-WM’s pretrained space to LeWM’s end-to-end SIGReg embeddings and noting that DINO-WM’s top PCs retain more state information, which interacts with Euclidean costs. It introduces SCALE, a training-time regularizer that aligns sampled latent pairwise distances with standardized task-state distances to induce DINO-like geometric properties in LeWM without replacing its encoder. Across five tasks, three solvers, and five compute budgets, SCALE consistently improves task–solver averages over LeWM, while a latent-to-state regression control achieves similar decodability but not distance alignment and yields less consistent planning gains, adding no planning-time overhead.
agents.why_it_matters: Shows that not just decodability but latent geometry (variance structure and distance alignment to state) materially affects JEPA planning quality, offering a lightweight regularizer to tune geometry for better planner performance.
agents.reason: Automated red-teaming framework that creates reusable, evolving attack 'skills' is highly relevant to scaling LLM security evaluations, red-team automation, and agentic attack surfaces.

agents.title: Towards a Risk Assessment of Malicious Skill Files in Coding Agents
agents.summary: The paper studies the attack surface introduced by agent skill folders in autonomous coding agents and presents an adversarial skill-synthesis method that converts 471 real shell commands into 2,826 benign-looking skills mapped to 11 ATT&CK tactics using six LLMs. It introduces a reproducible evaluation pipeline with stratification, evidence anchoring, refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override, using a three-judge LLM panel validated against a blind human gold standard (κ=0.85). In large-scale tests (5,629 runs), Gemini CLI was exploited in 95.5–96.1% and Qwen Code in 71.6–74.0% of runs with only 1.99% explicit safety recognition, and code/dataset are released at https://github.com/awsm-research/AgentJailbreak.
agents.why_it_matters: Provides a validated benchmark, eval pipeline, and high-base-rate exploitation evidence for skill-file attacks in coding agents—directly relevant to LLM security evals and agentic deployment risk.
agents.reason: Demonstrates pipeline attack surface in coding agents by hiding malicious shell commands in natural-language skill files — directly applicable to agentic-system attack vectors and red-teaming.

agents.title: Deployable Per-Instance Multi-Layer Activation Steering for Large Language Models
agents.summary: The paper shows that in activation steering, the optimal injection layers vary per input, with per-instance multi-layer selection outperforming any fixed global layer set across six binary persona traits on two 8B models. A greedy layer-ranking rule based on single-layer marginal effects nearly matches a per-instance oracle but requires gold labels, so the authors train a prompt-only predictor to mimic it and propose a deployable recipe: a prompt-based per-instance layer ranker, a classifier to infer steering direction, and an adaptive gate that limits layers by short steered passes. This deployable approach recovers most of the oracle’s gains, avoids dropping below unsteered baselines on average, reduces fluency collapse relative to strong global selection, and is supported by a mechanistic account emphasizing direction over magnitude that explains misdirection flips, collapse from over-steering, and unsteerable ceilings.
agents.why_it_matters: It operationalizes per-instance, label-free activation steering with adaptive multi-layer control, offering a practical path to safer, targeted behavior edits without sacrificing fluency—relevant to red-teaming defenses and controllable generation, and conceptually aligned with direction-based causal hypotheses familiar in interpretability.
agents.reason: Per-instance multi-layer activation steering directly targets editing/model control at inference time—relevant to attack/defense surfaces, deployment, and efficient selective interventions for LLM security and agent behavior.

agents.title: SkillsMetric: Mapping the Detection Boundary of Static Analysis for Malicious Agent Skills
agents.summary: This work introduces SkillsMetric, a five-stage static analysis framework that scores LLM agent skills across pattern density, statistical anomaly, dataflow taint, import anomaly, and capability mismatch. Using an adversarial dataset of 2,266 skills covering 16 attack types and the SkillMD-138K corpus, it reports AUC 0.93 and 5-fold CV F1 73.4%±0.5%, with 93% detection for data exfiltration and steganographic payloads. It also exposes blind spots—0% detection for host destruction via common shell commands and 42% for prompt injection—arguing static analysis alone is insufficient and should be paired with semantic review in defense-in-depth.
agents.why_it_matters: Directly maps the detection boundary of static analysis for agent skills, highlighting failure modes (e.g., prompt injection, host destruction) that inform red-teaming, hybrid detection pipelines, and security benchmarks for LLM agents.
agents.reason: Static analysis scoring of agent 'skills' maps to supply-chain and capability-based attack surfaces for LLM agents and helps red-teaming/defense of tool-augmented systems.

agents.title: Generating Attacks for LLMs with GFlowNets
