agents.summary: The work proposes an automated, human-independent red teaming framework that trains an attacker LLM via GFlowNets to probe a specified victim LLM and yield a quantitative robustness score. It addresses limitations of manual expert red teaming and automated methods tied to fixed datasets by enabling adaptive, creative attack generation. The approach targets generating more effective English adversarial inputs than existing benchmarks and, uniquely, introduces Turkish-language attack generation.
agents.why_it_matters: It explores GFlowNets for adaptive attack synthesis against LLMs, offering a path beyond fixed corpora and extending multilingual red teaming—a relevant direction for security evaluation and scalable adversarial data generation.
agents.reason: Uses GFlowNets to autogenerate adversarial attacks for LLM red‑teaming — directly relevant to scalable red‑teaming and attack generation for LLM security.

agents.title: Proving the Utility of Large Language Models in Cybersecurity Simulations: A Comprehensive Examination
agents.summary: The paper evaluates LLMs for cybersecurity simulations, using YAML to represent complex network configurations and to drive pipelines that support RL agent training. It compares LLM-based techniques to classical methods like Double Q-learning with PER, claiming improved efficiency, adaptability, and realism in cyberattack simulations. In benchmarks on multiple synthetic topologies, LLM-instantiated Python agents reached up to a 94.5% compromise rate and 0.02–0.06s per assessment, a ~25,000x–50,000x speedup over traditional RL cycles.
agents.why_it_matters: Shows LLM-driven generation/execution pipelines can massively accelerate cyber-sim training and evaluation, relevant to secure LLM autonomy and sim-to-real robustness for time-series/agentic models.
agents.reason: Large-scale experimental evaluation of indirect prompt injection across channels and payloads maps closely to prompt-injection/jailbreak threat modeling and red-teaming methodology.

agents.title: Proof-of-Execution Memory: Defending LLM Agents Against Forged-Reasoning Attacks by Verifying What Actually Happened
agents.summary: The paper shows that FARMA-style forged-reasoning attacks bypass SENTINEL completely when the forgery is merely reworded by another LLM, with evasion on the first try and higher success on stronger models (98–100% on GPT-4o/4o-mini vs. 44% on Llama-3.1-8B). It introduces Proof-of-Execution Memory (PoEM), a tamper-evident HMAC-chained ledger that records only actually executed safety steps and gates skips on ledger confirmation, avoiding memory inspection. Across three models and three scenarios, PoEM reduces attack success to 0% with near-zero false positives, minimal overhead, robustness to attacks on itself, and works unchanged in a LangChain agent, while SENTINEL causes 33–50% false positives on legitimate operations.
agents.why_it_matters: It reframes agent safety from brittle content heuristics to verifiable execution traces, offering a practical, low-overhead control point that scales with model capability and integrates with common agent stacks.
agents.reason: Directly relevant to agentic LLM security: describes FARMA forged-reasoning attack on agent memory and a defenses' limitations (SENTINEL), matching interest in agent attack surfaces and red-teaming/guardrail bypass.

agents.title: COMA: A Compositional Misleading Attack Class on Security-RAG, and a Causal Counterfactual Defense
agents.summary: The paper defines COMA, a class of compositional misleading attacks on Security-RAG where each retrieved document is true, instruction-free, non-contradictory, and benign, yet their composition misleads the model. They instantiate COMA via action-corruption (correct diagnosis but inferior remediation) and verdict-flip (exploitability destabilized via undecidable reachability), showing consistent success across five models, two synthetic domains, and a real CVE, with verdict-flip degrading but persisting with stronger models; both succeed when the key disambiguating fact must be inferred rather than read. They introduce CCD, a causal counterfactual defense auditing leave-one-out document influence to flag answers dominated by low-trust sources, localize attacker-controlled docs without false positives on benign controls, and catch influence-spreading adversaries via an aggregate variant, releasing attack seeds and a CCD reference implementation.
agents.why_it_matters: It tightens the threat model for security-RAG by showing composition-only attacks that evade standard defenses and offers a causal auditing tool that ML security and foundation model researchers can build on or stress-test.
agents.reason: Detecting vulnerability signals in model hidden activations speaks to prefill/internal-state monitoring as a defense against code vulnerabilities and new red-teaming/inspection methods.

agents.title: FedLNS: Leverage LayerNorm Signature Modeling to Mitigate Adversarial Manipulation in Federated LLMs
agents.summary: The paper introduces FedLNS, a server-side framework that screens federated LLM client updates by modeling changes in trainable normalization-layer parameters as signatures and comparing them to a history-aware cross-client reference. It operates without additional client-to-server metadata, raw client data, trusted server datasets, labeled attack examples, or a separately trained detector, and retains full-model updates for standard or compatible aggregation after screening. Experiments on GPT-, BERT-, and LLaMA-style models trained from scratch with 200 clients show that under 40% target manipulation, FedLNS yields lower test perplexity than six baselines across IID and non-IID partitions.
agents.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, data-free, model-internal signal for adversarial update filtering in federated LLM training, aligning with robustness and integrity concerns in LLM security.
agents.reason: FedLNS proposes a practical server-side defense against malicious client updates in federated LLM training—directly relevant to attack surfaces (poisoning, integrity) for deployed LLMs.

agents.title: Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
agents.summary: Auditing step-level credit signals against executed-replay causal ground truth in ALFWorld finds that LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, and policy confidence do not identify causally pivotal steps better than chance, despite performing against annotated correctness. Ground truth contribution is sparse and model-dependent, with substantial variation in counterfactual support across similar-scale policies, and implicit credit tracks policy fluency (high rank correlation) while outcome conditioning adds no causal information. A confidence-only router reduces judge cost modestly without improving pivotal-step detection, and a pre-registered seven-arm training study shows no reliable gains over the base policy, with observed differences attributable to training dose (effective sample size) rather than credit content, implying comparisons must control for dose.
agents.why_it_matters: It challenges common step-level credit proxies in agent training and evaluation, highlights the need for causal replay-based auditing, and warns that reported gains may be sample-size artifacts rather than better credit assignment.
agents.reason: Direct audit showing step-level credit signals fail to identify causally important agent steps — highly relevant to agent behavior evaluation, red-teaming, and training/credit assignment for tool-using LLM agents.

agents.title: RouteGuard: Certifying Routing Gain in LLM Multi-Agent Systems When Complementarity Is Not Enough
agents.summary: The paper shows that common assumptions for multi-agent LLM routing—optimizing gate AUC and relying on advisor complementarity—do not determine deployable gain, and introduces RouteGuard to certify routing benefit. It decomposes gain as G = πΔ_E, identifies a conditional-regret functional Φ as the governing quantity (not AUC), provides a finite-sample certification bracket with a matching Le Cam lower bound that is constant-sharp over the fixed-activity class, and observes a robustness phase transition. Experiments on RouterBench and OpenRCA demonstrate RouteGuard acting as a guardrail, certifying gain only under prompt-level sampling (not workload-cluster resampling) on RouterBench and refusing to certify on OpenRCA due to advisor redundancy, with pre-registered semi-synthetic controls confirming calibration thresholds.
agents.why_it_matters: It offers a principled, sample-sensitive certification of routing gain that can prevent illusory improvements in LLM multi-agent systems and aligns evaluation with deployment risk.
agents.reason: Analyzes routing certification in LLM multi-advisor systems and provides finite-sample guarantees for when routing yields deployable gain—relevant to safe agent composition, evaluation metrics beyond AUC, and deployment-risk assessment.

agents.title: TimeSage-EV: A Live Benchmark for Agentic Time Series Analysis in Evolving Environments
agents.summary: TimeSage-EV is a live benchmark for agentic time series analysis that evaluates temporal validity and cutoff-aware evidence use across 60 institutional scenarios and 1,485 scenario-period QA pairs from Feb 2023 to May 2026, spanning multiple release cadences. At each period, LLM agents receive time series data and source reports, with withheld target releases serving as ground truth, and are evaluated on state identification, data summarization, and outlook reasoning. Experiments with frontier LLM agents and TimeSage-1.0, a self-evolving agent with a reusable analytical skill library, show substantial performance gaps and recurring failures in temporal validity, exogenous context use, and adaptation, with monthly updates, code, a leaderboard, and failure-mode analyses released.
agents.why_it_matters: It offers a continuously updating, real-world benchmark to stress-test LLM agents’ temporal grounding and adaptability—key for secure, cutoff-aware forecasting and decision support in evolving time series contexts.
agents.reason: Analysis of when agent skills fail informs robustness and harness design for agentic systems and red-teaming; valuable for understanding failure modes though somewhat broad.

agents.title: Stopping and Routing LLM Judge Panels
agents.summary: The work frames judge-panel design as a role-conditioned allocation problem that, using a small labeled audit set, declared slices, and judge costs, estimates target-relative roles: copies, complements, and specialists. These roles yield a policy to drop copies, add complements globally, route specialists on slices, and stop when validation gain falls below a threshold, producing a reusable, auditable call plan. It is empirically compared across multiple audit settings against single judges, flat panels, diversity heuristics, full-call stacking, reliability juries, and frugal cascades, yielding a regime map for when to route specialists, stop in saturated regimes, keep broad ensembles, and ignore conditional copies.
agents.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete, auditable routing/early-stopping policy for multi-judge LLM evaluation that balances risk and cost across slices—directly relevant to secure deployment and panel design in LLM oversight and verifiers for time-series or reasoning tasks.
agents.reason: Optimizing which judges to call and when directly impacts scalable red-teaming, evaluation budgets, and LLM-as-judge pipelines relevant to security and agent verification.

agents.title: From Positionwise Confidence to Prefix Scheduling: Verifier Skipping in Speculative Decoding
agents.summary: The paper studies verifier skipping in speculative diffusion decoding, introducing a lossy policy that commits selected draft prefixes without invoking the target verifier and asks which confidence signal should schedule skips. It finds that better token predictors do not necessarily yield better schedulers because skipping needs contiguous high-confidence prefixes and short skips can add drafting rounds; it compares raw confidence with learned marginal and conditional survival scores under Strict SDD, lenience, and top-k acceptance baselines. On HumanEval with DiffuCoder-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-32B, all three signals reduce verifier calls by 9.6%–13.5% at the same observed pass@1 as Strict SDD, with raw confidence saving the most despite marginal survival having higher positionwise AUROC, leading to the conclusion that the core challenge is prefix scheduling rather than token prediction alone.
agents.why_it_matters: Introduces a new lossy control axis—prefix scheduling for verifier skips—that can cut inference cost in speculative decoding and reveals a counterintuitive gap between positionwise confidence metrics and online efficiency.
agents.reason: Speculative decoding verifier-skipping directly impacts LLM inference cost and decoding pipelines; relevant for efficient red-teaming and large-scale automated attacks/agents where verifier invocation is a bottleneck.

agents.title: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
agents.summary: The paper introduces HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization where an LLM optimizer iteratively edits a target agent’s harness under expensive, stochastic evaluation with a fixed budget, using only graded feedback and without access to a held-out test partition. A trusted execution environment enforces evaluation boundaries, meters resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit, and performance is measured by normalized gain over the seed harness. Evaluating five frontier LLMs across four tasks and 111 runs, the authors find optimizer models differentiate more than coding harnesses, native harnesses aren’t consistently superior, and gains vary substantially by task and seed regime, establishing harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with room for improvement.
agents.why_it_matters: It provides a rigorous, auditable setup to compare LLMs’ agentic self-improvement under realistic noisy/expensive evals—relevant for secure agent orchestration and optimizing time-series/tool-using pipelines.
agents.reason: Benchmark for optimizing agent harnesses is directly relevant to LLM agent security (attack surface via prompts/tools/orchestration) and offers an evaluation protocol useful for red-teaming and robust harness design.

agents.title: Trident : How to Break Deep Reinforcement Learning Cyber Defenses (Agentic)
agents.summary: The paper introduces Trident, an agentic LLM red-teaming framework for evaluating DRL-based cyber defenses, consisting of a dynamic benchmark across CybORG CAGE 4 and CyberWheel, a dataset of 13k+ red-blue trajectories for RLVR, and a Code-as-Policy RLVR architecture. Trident reframes red-agent training as a contextual bandit using a Log Summarizer–Planner–Coder pipeline, where a trainable Planner produces complete attack strategies from compressed logs and a frozen Coder turns them into executable Python policies against live DRL defenders. Empirically, a single 7B planner substantially degrades blue-agent performance (average 522% reduction vs. static red baselines) and uncovers emergent behaviors like decoy avoidance and adaptive state prioritization that static heuristics miss.
agents.why_it_matters: It demonstrates an RLVR-driven, code-generating agent that reliably breaks DRL cyber defenses and provides a benchmark/dataset, directly informing LLM security evaluation and agent robustness research.
agents.reason: Provides trajectory-level certification methods for modular LLM-based security agents, addressing guarantees and calibration across multi-stage pipelines — useful for safety evaluation of agentic security systems.

agents.title: Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning
agents.summary: The paper introduces Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies closed-form amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase alignment to retrieved past–future windows before feeding them to a frozen TSFM. On a frozen Chronos-Bolt, it outperforms a state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter across seven benchmark datasets (average −3.75% MSE), and it also improves zero-shot MSE by 2.5%–13.7% on four additional frozen TSFMs without per-backbone tuning. Analysis shows aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts in frozen backbones that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out futures-averaging, suggesting frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals.
agents.why_it_matters: It challenges the need for learned fusion in RAG for forecasting by showing closed-form alignment on frozen backbones yields SOTA gains and ridge-like in-context adaptation, a strong baseline relevant to LLM alignment and retrieval studies.
agents.reason: DASH improves on-policy self-distillation for reasoning models with temporally-adaptive supervision horizons — relevant to improving RL-style fine-tuning and evaluation of reasoning/judging behavior and scalable red-teaming.

agents.title: FutureBridge: Token Selection Beyond Local Preference in Collaborative Decoding
agents.summary: FutureBridge proposes a token reranking scheme for LLM–SLM collaborative decoding that prioritizes tokens enabling the SLM’s subsequent reasoning rather than the LLM’s local preference. Training uses an answer-verified LLM trajectory to fix a shared future, while a frozen SLM assigns counterfactual scores to candidate tokens under this common context to supervise a lightweight reranker observing only the current state and token. At inference, the LLM only expands the candidate pool and the reranker selects a single token before handing generation back to the SLM without appending any future suffix, yielding a 35.1% relative Math Avg. improvement for Qwen3-1.7B across five math reasoning benchmarks over greedy decoding.
agents.why_it_matters: It reframes collaboration as SLM-aware token selection, offering a practical path to safer, stronger small-model reasoning with minimal LLM involvement—relevant to alignment, tool-use gating, and cost/security tradeoffs in cooperative decoding.
agents.reason: FutureBridge proposes collaborative decoding between LLM and smaller models to improve SLM reasoning—relevant for efficient red-teaming, agent pipelines, and attack/defense strategies where token choice affects downstream agent behavior.

agents.title: Intern-S2-Preview: Scientific Agentic Foundation Model
agents.summary: Intern-S2-Preview introduces scientific agentic foundation models trained via multimodal pretraining on rendered scientific documents, interleaved image-text, and diverse scientific corpora, followed by a unified post-training stack of SFT, scalable multi-task RL, black- and white-box agentic RL, and on-policy distillation. The pipeline adds practical rollout/training techniques—partial rollout with off-policy correction, adaptive length regularization, online speculative decoding, robust multi-task optimization, and trace-aware experience assembly—and explores architecture-level extensions: a 397B model with time series modules for efficient long-sequence understanding and numerical forecasting, plus a separate Memory Decoder path for rapid specialization without changing the frozen backbone. Evaluations report competitive or leading results across scientific, multimodal, agentic, and general-purpose benchmarks, with time-series gains on SciTS and a MemDec-4B extension improving Biology-Instructions average from 56.92 to 60.32 without modifying the 397B backbone.
agents.why_it_matters: Brings a concrete agentic RL + multimodal + TS forecasting stack with stability tricks and a memory-augmented specialization path relevant to secure tool-use agents and time-series LLMs.
agents.reason: Agentic multimodal scientific foundation model work intersects with agentic-system attack surfaces and long-horizon reasoning, relevant for security analysis though not focused on adversarial robustness.

agents.title: Learning What to Fail On: Failure-Mode Contextual Bandits for Adversarial Data Curation
agents.summary: The paper frames adversarial data curation as a failure-mode contextual bandit: RAG generates candidates, the target model filters them, an LLM judge ensemble validates them, and clustering groups recurring failure modes. A stochastic policy samples failure modes for retraining using a validation-based reward that trades off robustness gains, forgetting, and data cost, yielding consistent gains over prior adversarial augmentation on SNLI, ANLI, MultiNLI, and transfer to FEVER with RoBERTa variants. They also provide a theoretical interpretation that failure-mode sampling reduces shortcut-aligned gradient contributions while bounding distributional drift, enabling scalable robustness improvements without human annotation.
agents.why_it_matters: It operationalizes adaptive, failure-driven data selection with bandit control and LLM-judged RAG—useful for red-teaming LLMs and for principled, cost-aware adversarial curation relevant to secure training and time-series-style foundation data pipelines.
agents.reason: Adversarial data curation via failure-mode contextual bandits targets robustness of NLU models and retrieval-augmented synthetic-data pipelines—highly relevant to scalable red-teaming and adversarial training for LLMs.

agents.title: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
agents.summary: DreamGuard is a proactive runtime guardrail for LLM agents that uses a risk-aware world model to track a compact recurrent latent state over trajectories and forecast future latent states. From these forecasts, it derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence and fuses multi-horizon signals to decide on interventions before tool executions. Across four benchmarks and an online evaluation, DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive baselines with the best safety-utility trade-off and averages 25 ms end-to-end latency per call.
agents.why_it_matters: Introduces a trajectory-aware, low-latency guardrail with explicit risk modeling, aligning with interests in long-horizon safety for LLM agents and bridging to sequence modeling ideas from time series foundation models.
agents.reason: Adaptive allocation across model populations for LLM-driven evolutionary search is relevant for cost-efficient red-teaming/evolutionary program search, but more about budgeting than core security.

agents.title: Learning the Pareto Frontier of Predictive Models under Distribution Shift
agents.summary: The paper introduces Frontier Learning, which treats a library of pretrained models with mixed access regimes (black-box predictions and white-box representations) as complementary sources under distribution shift. It builds a unified target-domain feature by concatenating internal representations from white-box models with outputs from black-box models, then trains a lightweight regularized supervised learner, guaranteeing training-sample risk no worse than any single baseline including zero-shot reuse, fine-tuning, or direct training. Experiments on simulations and real-world shifts (DomainNet/VisDA and MIMIC-IV-Notes ICU mortality) show it matches or outperforms the strongest individual reuse strategy, with the largest gains when no single baseline is reliable across the shifts considered.
agents.why_it_matters: Provides a simple, access-agnostic ensemble-on-representations approach that subsumes common reuse strategies and is empirically strong under shift—relevant to robustness/security and modular reuse of foundation models.
agents.reason: Agentic BO using LLMs to inject priors into optimization touches on agentic systems and leveraging LLMs as components—relevant to attack/defense surfaces and efficient automated red-teaming workflows.

agents.title: Palmyra x6 Technical Report: An Agentic, Tool-Use Model Post-Trained via Anchored Supervised Fine-Tuning
agents.summary: Palmyra x6 is an enterprise-focused agentic LLM post-trained from an MoE base using Anchored Supervised Fine-Tuning on 626 verified synthetic tool-use trajectories, run for a single epoch with a low LR and a KL anchor to the frozen base, optimized via a Muon+Adam hybrid. It delivers substantial gains for the Writer Agent and compares favorably on public benchmarks, achieving the top BFCL Core score of 0.785 and the highest six-benchmark mean among its cohort. The model is also competitive or leading in the authors’ bias and safety evaluations relative to comparators.
agents.why_it_matters: Tight, KL-anchored post-training on compact synthetic tool-use traces yielding SOTA-ish agentic performance is directly relevant to secure tool-use alignment and data-efficient post-training strategies for robust, controllable agents.
agents.reason: Agentic tool-use fine-tuning recipe and anchored SFT on a MoE base is relevant to agent design and deployment risk, though it's an engineering report rather than security-first research.

agents.title: No Gaussian Required: Contrastive Inverse Dynamics for JEPA World Models
agents.summary: The paper proposes Action-Contrastive Masked Transition Modeling (AC-MTM) for JEPA world models, replacing LeWM’s SIGReg Gaussian latent regularizer with a training-only inverse-dynamics head optimized via Action-NCE to prevent representation collapse. This contrastive inverse branch ensures each latent transition identifies its generating action among batch negatives, is discarded after training, and leaves test-time behavior identical to LeWM. AC-MTM matches SIGReg on four standard pixel-control tasks under a matched planner and substantially outperforms it on OGBench Visual Scene (80.0±2.0% vs 58.0±2.0%), suggesting prescribed latent geometry can bottleneck performance; code is released at the provided GitHub link.
agents.why_it_matters: It offers a distribution-free, target-network-free anti-collapse mechanism for JEPA-style world models that scales to harder visual control, directly relevant to secure, robust representation learning without prescriptive latent priors.
agents.reason: JEPA world-model work on contrastive inverse dynamics may inform representation objectives useful for time-series or sequential modeling, but it's primarily a world-model / vision-style contribution rather than TSFM security.

efficiency.title: Who Verifies the Benchmark? Decentralizing Trust in Large Language Model Evaluation
efficiency.summary: The paper argues that LLM evaluation lacks verifiability and is vulnerable to unverified vendor claims and LLM-judge identity bias, with real-world consequences highlighted by the January 27, 2025 market panic. Using seven verifier models, it measures how disclosing the source model identity shifts scores across 58 factual, reasoning, political, and preference tasks, finding minimal effects on factual items, moderate effects on stress-reasoning, and large effects on geopolitically sensitive topics, with examples including GLM 5.1 (+7.00, p=0.0249) and Llama 3.3 70B (+1.56, p=0.00). It proposes a blockchain-based commit–reveal protocol with Autonomous Economic Agents to create an on-chain, tamper-evident audit trail that separates blind evaluation from post-hoc claims and eases verification for researchers and leaderboard operators.
efficiency.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to LLM security and evaluation: quantifies identity-aware judge bias across sensitive tasks and offers a verifiable, decentralized commit–reveal protocol that could harden benchmark integrity and leaderboards.
efficiency.reason: Model editing for secure code generation evaluates model-level hardening methods versus inference-time approaches — relevant to reducing malicious or vulnerable generations in deployed LLMs.

efficiency.title: From Positionwise Confidence to Prefix Scheduling: Verifier Skipping in Speculative Decoding
efficiency.summary: The paper studies verifier skipping in speculative diffusion decoding, introducing a lossy policy that commits selected draft prefixes without invoking the target verifier and asks which confidence signal should schedule skips. It finds that better token predictors do not necessarily yield better schedulers because skipping needs contiguous high-confidence prefixes and short skips can add drafting rounds; it compares raw confidence with learned marginal and conditional survival scores under Strict SDD, lenience, and top-k acceptance baselines. On HumanEval with DiffuCoder-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-32B, all three signals reduce verifier calls by 9.6%–13.5% at the same observed pass@1 as Strict SDD, with raw confidence saving the most despite marginal survival having higher positionwise AUROC, leading to the conclusion that the core challenge is prefix scheduling rather than token prediction alone.
efficiency.why_it_matters: Introduces a new lossy control axis—prefix scheduling for verifier skips—that can cut inference cost in speculative decoding and reveals a counterintuitive gap between positionwise confidence metrics and online efficiency.
efficiency.reason: Speculative decoding verifier-skipping directly impacts LLM inference cost and decoding pipelines; relevant for efficient red-teaming and large-scale automated attacks/agents where verifier invocation is a bottleneck.

efficiency.title: FutureBridge: Token Selection Beyond Local Preference in Collaborative Decoding
efficiency.summary: FutureBridge proposes a token reranking scheme for LLM–SLM collaborative decoding that prioritizes tokens enabling the SLM’s subsequent reasoning rather than the LLM’s local preference. Training uses an answer-verified LLM trajectory to fix a shared future, while a frozen SLM assigns counterfactual scores to candidate tokens under this common context to supervise a lightweight reranker observing only the current state and token. At inference, the LLM only expands the candidate pool and the reranker selects a single token before handing generation back to the SLM without appending any future suffix, yielding a 35.1% relative Math Avg. improvement for Qwen3-1.7B across five math reasoning benchmarks over greedy decoding.
efficiency.why_it_matters: It reframes collaboration as SLM-aware token selection, offering a practical path to safer, stronger small-model reasoning with minimal LLM involvement—relevant to alignment, tool-use gating, and cost/security tradeoffs in cooperative decoding.
efficiency.reason: FutureBridge proposes collaborative decoding between LLM and smaller models to improve SLM reasoning—relevant for efficient red-teaming, agent pipelines, and attack/defense strategies where token choice affects downstream agent behavior.

efficiency.title: Tevatron-Elastic: A Unified Abstraction for Training Elastic Retrievers and Rerankers
efficiency.summary: Tevatron-Elastic introduces a unified abstraction that encapsulates three orthogonal elasticity axes for IR models—fewer layers, upper-layer token pruning, and shorter embeddings—so a single checkpoint supports multiple runtime sizes selected via a schedule. The abstraction applies uniformly to retrievers and rerankers, encoder and decoder backbones via HF interfaces, subsuming prior methods like Matryoshka embeddings, early exit, 2D Matryoshka (e.g., Starbucks), and layerwise token compression, and also enables Matryoshka LTC for jointly training multiple token-compression ratios in one retriever. Empirically, across 20 checkpoints, three backbones, and two tasks, they report smooth quality curves, near-single-size training cost, and controlled wallclock speedups, releasing the framework and checkpoints for elastic retrieval systems.
efficiency.why_it_matters: A clean, composable interface for multi-axis elasticity in retrievers/rerankers simplifies deployment-time cost/quality trade-offs and unifies techniques ML security and systems folks already use (early exit, Matryoshka, token compression) under one training/checkpoint regime.
efficiency.reason: Elastic retrievers/rerankers address scalable retrieval tradeoffs and dynamic model-size/runtime adaptation—useful for efficient RAG/agent pipelines and evaluation of retrieval components in security workflows.

efficiency.title: Can a Lightweight Multimodal Model Estimate LLM Reasoning Performance? A Study for Compute-Optimal Document Inference
efficiency.summary: The paper introduces BudgetDoc, a multimodal benchmark with explicit supervision for model-budget-performance trade-offs on three document tasks, addressing the cost and over-thinking issues of uniform inference budgets in LLMs. Using BudgetDoc, the authors train DRB, a ~1B-parameter pre-flight estimator (SigLIP-2 + Qwen3-0.6B) that predicts ordinal model performance across budget levels with a weighted F1 of 0.753. DRB enables dynamic reasoning budget allocation across five frontier models and three datasets, matching or improving F1 over always-maximum-budget baselines in 9/15 settings while reducing cost, and shows preliminary promise for cross-model selection generalization.
efficiency.why_it_matters: It offers a practical path to compute-optimal, layout-aware reasoning allocation and model selection for document tasks, directly relevant to secure and efficient deployment of reasoning LLMs.
efficiency.reason: A lightweight multimodal estimator to predict LLM reasoning performance (compute-budget tradeoffs) is useful for compute-optimal allocation and efficient red-teaming at scale, relevant to security/serving tradeoffs.

efficiency.title: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
efficiency.summary: DreamGuard is a proactive runtime guardrail for LLM agents that uses a risk-aware world model to track a compact recurrent latent state over trajectories and forecast future latent states. From these forecasts, it derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence and fuses multi-horizon signals to decide on interventions before tool executions. Across four benchmarks and an online evaluation, DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive baselines with the best safety-utility trade-off and averages 25 ms end-to-end latency per call.
efficiency.why_it_matters: Introduces a trajectory-aware, low-latency guardrail with explicit risk modeling, aligning with interests in long-horizon safety for LLM agents and bridging to sequence modeling ideas from time series foundation models.
efficiency.reason: Adaptive allocation across model populations for LLM-driven evolutionary search is relevant for cost-efficient red-teaming/evolutionary program search, but more about budgeting than core security.

efficiency.title: Learning the Pareto Frontier of Predictive Models under Distribution Shift
efficiency.summary: The paper introduces Frontier Learning, which treats a library of pretrained models with mixed access regimes (black-box predictions and white-box representations) as complementary sources under distribution shift. It builds a unified target-domain feature by concatenating internal representations from white-box models with outputs from black-box models, then trains a lightweight regularized supervised learner, guaranteeing training-sample risk no worse than any single baseline including zero-shot reuse, fine-tuning, or direct training. Experiments on simulations and real-world shifts (DomainNet/VisDA and MIMIC-IV-Notes ICU mortality) show it matches or outperforms the strongest individual reuse strategy, with the largest gains when no single baseline is reliable across the shifts considered.
efficiency.why_it_matters: Provides a simple, access-agnostic ensemble-on-representations approach that subsumes common reuse strategies and is empirically strong under shift—relevant to robustness/security and modular reuse of foundation models.
efficiency.reason: Agentic BO using LLMs to inject priors into optimization touches on agentic systems and leveraging LLMs as components—relevant to attack/defense surfaces and efficient automated red-teaming workflows.

efficiency.title: Task-Conditioned Least-Privilege Learning for Executable Terminal and MCP Agents
efficiency.summary: The paper introduces a post-training framework to teach a 4B LLM to select task-conditioned authority in executable terminal and MCP settings, complementing permission gates and sandboxing. It uses deterministic verifiers auditing actions pre- and post-execution along six risk dimensions, combined with task-specific sufficient-authority envelopes to compute excess-privilege signals for optimization, and is trained on Qwen3.5-4B over 1,500 tasks. On 500 held-out tasks (2,896 episodes) the trained model achieves 98.48% safe success vs. 64.36% for the base policy and reduces excess-authority errors from 4.56% to 0.79%, with external tests showing capability retention/prompt-directed improvement and a 400-task continuation indicating generalization with a 6.99 pp reduction in excess-authority events.
efficiency.why_it_matters: It proposes and empirically validates a least-privilege post-training signal for tool-use agents, directly addressing excess-authority risks in executable/MCP settings without degrading capabilities.
efficiency.reason: Two-stage distillation of tabular foundation models into lightweight predictors is relevant for efficient deployment of foundation-style models, though focused on tabular rather than time-series.

efficiency.title: Pre-Compiled Pipeline Shards for Distributed LLM Inference on Intel AI PC Fleets
efficiency.summary: The work demonstrates pipeline-parallel LLM inference across Intel AI PCs by pre-compiling per-layer shards into OpenVINO graphs, with each node running a shard and passing activations onward. They recover monolithic performance by inserting a beam_idx Gather to trigger OpenVINO’s IndirectKVCache fusion, and further improve throughput via speculative decoding and interleaved multi-user micro-batching. Results: a two-node Llama 3.1 8B INT4 pipeline achieves 1.79x the single-user throughput of the unsplit model for two concurrent users and scales to a four-node deployment serving a 70B model with token-identical outputs to non-speculative decoding; code and scripts are provided.
efficiency.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, reproducible recipe to turn idle consumer AI PCs into a distributed LLM serving pool using pipeline sharding with OpenVINO, including concrete tricks (fusion trigger, speculative decoding, interleaved caching) and measured gains.
efficiency.reason: Distributed pipeline-parallel inference across Intel AI PCs is relevant to efficient serving and edge deployment for LLMs (useful for cheap red-teaming at scale), but not security or TSFM research.

evaluation.title: Toward Metacognitive One-Shot Indirect Prompt Injection: Strategy Abstraction Via Outcome-Conditioned Reflection
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces SAVOR, a one-shot IPI attack framework that moves adaptation offline via outcome-conditioned reflection over successful and failed trajectories from disjoint training environments, consolidating validated, context-conditioned strategies into a reusable strategy memory. At test time, the frozen memory generates a single payload per unseen target without iterative interaction or feedback, achieving the highest average attack success rate across two benchmarks and three victim models. On Agent Security Bench and the new executable OpenClaw-IPI, SAVOR outperforms the strongest prior attack by 2.5–11.8 points and beats the same injection channel without strategy learning by 23.1 and 28.6 points respectively, with learned memory transferring across defenses.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Demonstrates practical one-shot IPI via offline strategy distillation that generalizes across tools, goals, and defenses—relevant for red-teaming LLM agents and for designing defenses that hold under realistic single-interaction constraints.
evaluation.reason: One-shot indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks on tool-using agents via offline strategy distillation directly targets agentic attack surfaces and realistic attacker models—highly relevant to LLM security and red-teaming methodology.

evaluation.title: From Runnable to Verifiable: An Independent Reproducibility Study of LLM/Agent-Driven Vulnerability Validation Artifacts
evaluation.summary: This pre-registered reproducibility audit examines LLM/agent-driven vulnerability validation artifacts across 104 papers (2023–2026), finding only 59 with publicly reachable artifacts and executing 18 paper-level workflows and 102 anchor benchmark cases. It reports high mismatch and fragility: 58/102 anchor cases have internal CVE IDs diverging from directory labels; only 10/18 artifacts run end-to-end at R0 (11/18 after R1 env-only fixes); and embedded oracles are unreliable, with 20/30 patched-counterfactuals still signaling and 7/19 negative controls triggering, yielding oracle sensitivity 60% and specificity 45%. The study argues that vulnerable-build triggers are not CVE-specific evidence without a clean patched counterfactual and offers a reusable, pre-registered protocol (post-conditions, R0/R1 repair ladder, G1–G3 evidence levels, patched-counterfactual oracles) for the community.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It surfaces concrete failure modes and a reusable protocol for verifying LLM/agent security claims—directly informing eval design, oracle construction, and counterfactual controls for both LLM security and time-series-style benchmark reproducibility.
evaluation.reason: ActBench proposes an execution-trajectory-based behavioral safety benchmark for cowork agents, directly applicable to evaluating agent risks like data leakage and unauthorized actions—highly relevant for tooling and red-teaming.

evaluation.title: ElasticBack: Stealthy Conditional Backdoor in LLM-Agent Skills via Coupled Trigger-Rule Optimization
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces ElasticBack, a conditional single-skill backdoor for LLM agents that couples a malicious rule R in the skill document with a benign-looking trigger T in user queries, activating only when both appear. It constructs R via semantic-anchored rule injection and then fixes R while evolving T using a stealth-constrained genetic search to optimize attack effectiveness and stealth without modifying model weights. Experiments over three target behaviors (50 skills each) and four agent LLMs show high ASR with near-zero FPR, preserved clean accuracy, cross-model transfer, and evasion of deployment-time defenses, motivating stronger supply-chain defenses for skills.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Highlights a practical, weight-free, conditional backdoor vector in the emerging agent skill ecosystem, relevant to securing tool-using LLMs and evaluating defenses against stealthy trigger-rule couplings.
evaluation.reason: Presents a stealthy conditional backdoor attack targeting agent skills (supply-chain threat) with low-cost single-skill triggers—highly relevant to LLM agent security, tool/skill poisoning, and defense evaluation.

evaluation.title: On Understanding, Identifying, and Mitigating Vulnerabilities in Agentic Large Language Models
evaluation.summary: This paper reviews 85 papers (2023–2025) on security of agentic LLMs, selected via a PRISMA 2020 systematic process from 743 records, finding attack work outpaces defenses by 3.9:1. It reports that perception-layer vulnerabilities (prompt injection, jailbreaking, adversarial perturbations) dominate at 66%, while action-layer issues (tool misuse, code injection, sandbox escape) are only 4.7%, with code execution at 3.5% and tool-augmented agents at 12%. The authors propose a four-layer taxonomy (perception, brain, action, interaction) covering 13 vulnerability types, identify seven open problems focused on containment, and argue that weak isolation and architectural coupling let failures propagate across layers.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It quantifies where current security work is misaligned with real agentic risk surfaces and offers a layered taxonomy and containment-focused agenda that can guide rigorous evaluations and defenses for tool-using, code-executing LLM agents.
evaluation.reason: Systematic review focused on vulnerabilities unique to agentic LLMs (tool use, persistent memory, state changes) directly matches the reader's primary interest in agent attack surfaces and red‑teaming.

evaluation.title: Security Assessment of DeepSeek Harness with A.I.G: Evaluating Resistance to Indirect Prompt Injection
evaluation.summary: This work evaluates indirect prompt injection against DeepSeek Harness using AI-Infra-Guard to generate tests, deliver controlled taint across 16 channels and two carrier modes, run 14,560 executions, and analyze traces with both rule-based and LLM-based judges. The strongest observed attack success rates are 17.0% under LLMJudge for a fake-completion attack (text), 25.5% under RuleJudge for hidden Unicode (file), and 16.0% under RuleJudge for the skills channel (file), with LLMJudge assigning more partial compliance than RuleJudge (7.3% vs. 2.0%). The study connects outcomes to DSH’s handling of tool results, extra contexts, and tool-call policy hooks, and proposes controls between untrusted content and sensitive actions, with code released at the linked repository.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Provides a large-scale, reproducible, channel- and payload-stratified benchmark of indirect prompt injection on an agentic LLM stack with dual judges, informing defense design and evaluation baselines.
evaluation.reason: Black-box auditing of vendor-hosted LLM APIs via statistical repeated-query testing is highly relevant for red-teaming, API threat models, and evaluation methodology.

evaluation.title: Foundation Agents Meet Agentic Deep Research: Evidence-Grounded Clinical Code Forecasting
evaluation.summary: The paper tackles prospective multi-label next-encounter ICD forecasting by composing structured EHR and language foundation models with medical search and ICD dictionaries in a DeepResearch workflow called ICD-Deepresearch. It uses SparseEHR to create an EHR Prior for bounded research expansion, integrates an independent GPT-5 Direct Forecast for complementary candidates, and performs final validation/dedup/ranking with separate rationale generation that doesn’t alter predictions. On MIMIC-III/IV it reports patient-averaged precision/recall of 24.60/35.09% and 25.14/48.32%, and physicians rate its retrieved documents more useful than standalone GPT-5 web search and Medical Deep Research, with improvements over registered local comparators.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Demonstrates an agentic, evidence-grounded composition of EHR and LLM predictors that yields measurable gains in future-code forecasting and retrieval usefulness—relevant to secure, auditable multi-agent workflows for clinical time-series forecasting.
evaluation.reason: COMA describes subtle RAG attacks where benign, factual docs mislead security copilots — highly relevant to RAG poisoning, red-teaming, and security copilots.

evaluation.title: LiveHouse-TS: An Open-world Living Benchmark for Time Series Foundation Models
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces LiveHouse-TS, an open-world, living benchmark infrastructure for evaluating TSFMs via prequential testing on real future data rather than static windows. It shifts evaluation focus from snapshot accuracy to continuous temporal validity in environments with seasonality, distribution shifts, and unexpected events, aiming to answer long-term questions about ranking stability and robustness. Streaming evaluations across 11 domains and 17 datasets show that model rankings from static benchmarks dramatically reshuffle under the live protocol.
evaluation.why_it_matters: If you work on LLM security or TSFMs, this exposes how static benchmarks can mislead robustness assessments under shifts, offering an infrastructure to stress-test models’ long-term validity—analogous to live red-teaming and continual evals in LLMs.
evaluation.reason: Directly targets time-series foundation models with a new open-world benchmark capturing distribution shift and continual evaluation — highly relevant to zero-shot/few-shot forecasting, long-horizon robustness, and realistic evaluation methodology.

evaluation.title: CLaST: Context-aware Contrastive VAE for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
evaluation.summary: The paper proposes CLaST, a contrastive VAE for probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting that learns context-preserving embeddings via a contrastive loss. It targets the limitation of deep generative forecasters that fail to capture internal temporal dependencies, leading to weak latent representations. Across nine benchmarks, CLaST outperforms strong baselines with up to 16.4% CRPS and 14.4% NMAE gains on short-term tasks, and up to 48.6% CRPS and 25.1% NMAE gains on long-term tasks.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Shows that contrastive objectives inside generative forecasters can materially sharpen latent dynamics and probabilistic accuracy, informing representation design for robust sequence modeling and safety-relevant uncertainty calibration.
evaluation.reason: Scale-aware pretraining across heterogeneous sampling frequencies addresses a core TSFM pretraining objective (cross-dataset transfer, patching) and proposes representation alignment — highly relevant to the reader's primary TSFM interests.

evaluation.title: SCALE: State-Calibrated Latent Embeddings for JEPA Planning in the Right Geometry
evaluation.summary: The paper studies JEPA-style planning where terminal embedding costs depend on representation geometry, comparing DINO-WM’s pretrained space to LeWM’s end-to-end SIGReg embeddings and noting that DINO-WM’s top PCs retain more state information, which interacts with Euclidean costs. It introduces SCALE, a training-time regularizer that aligns sampled latent pairwise distances with standardized task-state distances to induce DINO-like geometric properties in LeWM without replacing its encoder. Across five tasks, three solvers, and five compute budgets, SCALE consistently improves task–solver averages over LeWM, while a latent-to-state regression control achieves similar decodability but not distance alignment and yields less consistent planning gains, adding no planning-time overhead.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Shows that not just decodability but latent geometry (variance structure and distance alignment to state) materially affects JEPA planning quality, offering a lightweight regularizer to tune geometry for better planner performance.
evaluation.reason: Automated red-teaming framework that creates reusable, evolving attack 'skills' is highly relevant to scaling LLM security evaluations, red-team automation, and agentic attack surfaces.

evaluation.title: Enhancing Anomaly Resilience in Research Networks: A Large-Scale Forecasting Benchmark for Dynamic Security Baselining
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces a high-fidelity traffic forecasting framework to create dynamic security baselines for RENs, addressing the challenge that elephant flows resemble volumetric attacks to conventional monitors. Using a 57-day Internet2 dataset (13.7B packets across ten backbone routers), it benchmarks six forecasting model families, including SARIMA and long-sequence architectures (TiDE, PatchTST), over 960 configurations. Results show advanced models—especially TiDE—reduce baseline prediction error by 30–42% (p < 0.001) and that a new anomaly-integration strategy yields a 3.3% robustness gain under noise, improving separation of scientific bursts from anomalies.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It provides a statistically validated, large-scale benchmark showing long-sequence LLM-adjacent forecasters (e.g., TiDE/PatchTST) materially improve dynamic baselining for REN security, informing robust anomaly detection under bursty traffic.
evaluation.reason: AMS detects safety-training modifications via activation geometry across major model families—highly pertinent to model integrity, detection of fine-tune/backdoor changes and LLM security for deployed models.

evaluation.title: When Do PEFT Adaptations Leak Structure? Measuring Black-Box Structural Bounds in Public-Base Model Services
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces VectorHijack-SR, a black-box measurement method that turns paired victim/base residuals into calibrated bounds over PEFT family, layer locality, and coarse rank, using aggregated query-level statistics and a service-disjoint classifier plus a cross-fitted hierarchical rejector to test LoRA-manifold membership. Empirically, family leakage exceeds chance across multiple backbones/tasks, rank inference varies by task, the rejector attains AUROC 0.804 and high known-set accuracy but struggles with structurally close DoRA/LoRA+head, and exact-version linkage on held-out LoRA-r64 services reaches AUC 0.940. Despite measurable structural leakage, experiments show a visibility–exploitability gap: two-stage recovery offers no fair-budget query savings, posterior-selected PEFT underperforms distill-then-convert PEFT, and free-running generation remains near chance.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It provides concrete, black-box evidence and metrics for structural leakage from PEFTed services with known bases, informing red-team audits, model fingerprinting, and security evaluations of adapter deployment choices.
evaluation.reason: Directly studies information leakage from PEFT adapters in public-base services — highly relevant to model extraction, PIi leakage, and red-team measurement for LLM security.

evaluation.title: An Empirical Study of Output-to-Input Loops for Black-Box Backdoor Detection in Fine-Tuned Open-Weight LLMs
evaluation.summary: The paper proposes self-feeding, a black-box test that recursively feeds a model’s outputs back as inputs to drift toward fine-tuning data, enabling backdoor discovery without training data, clean baselines, or trigger knowledge. Evaluated on six open-weight LLMs (3B–15B) with eleven backdoor categories and twenty prompts over up to ten steps, self-feeding detects backdoors in five models with 92.0% pooled precision, while a same-prompt baseline succeeds on only one of 120 prompt-model pairs; some prompts (jokes, arithmetic, coffee recipes) reach triggers in a few steps. Despite low per-prompt recall (19.2%), multi-prompt use raises model-level detection, though one model never triggers and there are two false positives; truncating to four steps preserves 100% model-level precision and cuts queries by 60%.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Offers a cheap, black-box, text-only stress test that surfaces fine-tune data modes (including backdoors) via output-to-input loops, complementing existing evals for open-weight LLMs and informing detection strategies for security-focused and time-series-style iterative generation analyses.
evaluation.reason: Black‑box self‑feeding method for detecting backdoors in fine‑tuned open LLMs is directly applicable to model vetting, backdoor detection, and practical security checks for deployed models.

evaluation.title: Generating Attacks for LLMs with GFlowNets
evaluation.summary: The work proposes an automated, human-independent red teaming framework that trains an attacker LLM via GFlowNets to probe a specified victim LLM and yield a quantitative robustness score. It addresses limitations of manual expert red teaming and automated methods tied to fixed datasets by enabling adaptive, creative attack generation. The approach targets generating more effective English adversarial inputs than existing benchmarks and, uniquely, introduces Turkish-language attack generation.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It explores GFlowNets for adaptive attack synthesis against LLMs, offering a path beyond fixed corpora and extending multilingual red teaming—a relevant direction for security evaluation and scalable adversarial data generation.
evaluation.reason: Uses GFlowNets to autogenerate adversarial attacks for LLM red‑teaming — directly relevant to scalable red‑teaming and attack generation for LLM security.

evaluation.title: Measuring Task-Agnostic Training Data Influence Across Language Model Pretraining
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces a task-agnostic measure of training data influence that quantifies how much an example’s gradient update reduces the squared distance to a run’s final parameters, estimated from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applied to 18 Pythia and PolyPythia configurations, the method reveals systematic temporal shifts in influential data: literature-related data align more with the parameter trajectory early, while STEM data align more later. This qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across configurations, offering a tractable trajectory-level perspective that complements task-based influence analyses.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Gives a practical, retraining-free way to map which data sources steer pretraining trajectories over time, informing data curation, curriculum, and security-relevant provenance audits for LLMs.
evaluation.reason: Proposes a task-agnostic measure of individual-example influence during LM pretraining which is highly relevant to data provenance, extraction/attribution, contamination, and training-time attack/defense analysis.

evaluation.title: The More Popular, The Harder to Forget: Adaptive Popularity for LLM Unlearning
evaluation.summary: The paper observes that popular facts are memorized more deeply in LLM pretraining and are harder to unlearn, while prior unlearning methods apply uniform gradient pressure regardless of frequency. It proposes AdaPop, which scales unlearning pressure using local token confidence and a per-fact popularity-dependent exponent from an external proxy, and uses a dual-ascent controller to automatically tune the retain penalty each epoch. On three model families and two benchmarks, AdaPop reduces leakage of forgotten content by ~5x on paraphrases and ~1.6x on adversarial reformulations, with internal metrics showing larger divergence from pre-unlearning states on the forget set and closer retention on the retain set compared to baselines.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Targets frequency-aware unlearning with automated retain/forget control, improving robustness to paraphrase/adversarial probes—relevant for red-teaming, safety fine-tuning, and deployment-time data governance.
evaluation.reason: Directly tackles unlearning/memorization—a core LLM security concern (data extraction, forgetting) with a practical adaptive method and measured leakage improvements.

evaluation.title: Proving the Utility of Large Language Models in Cybersecurity Simulations: A Comprehensive Examination
evaluation.summary: The paper evaluates LLMs for cybersecurity simulations, using YAML to represent complex network configurations and to drive pipelines that support RL agent training. It compares LLM-based techniques to classical methods like Double Q-learning with PER, claiming improved efficiency, adaptability, and realism in cyberattack simulations. In benchmarks on multiple synthetic topologies, LLM-instantiated Python agents reached up to a 94.5% compromise rate and 0.02–0.06s per assessment, a ~25,000x–50,000x speedup over traditional RL cycles.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Shows LLM-driven generation/execution pipelines can massively accelerate cyber-sim training and evaluation, relevant to secure LLM autonomy and sim-to-real robustness for time-series/agentic models.
evaluation.reason: Large-scale experimental evaluation of indirect prompt injection across channels and payloads maps closely to prompt-injection/jailbreak threat modeling and red-teaming methodology.

evaluation.title: Proof-of-Execution Memory: Defending LLM Agents Against Forged-Reasoning Attacks by Verifying What Actually Happened
evaluation.summary: The paper shows that FARMA-style forged-reasoning attacks bypass SENTINEL completely when the forgery is merely reworded by another LLM, with evasion on the first try and higher success on stronger models (98–100% on GPT-4o/4o-mini vs. 44% on Llama-3.1-8B). It introduces Proof-of-Execution Memory (PoEM), a tamper-evident HMAC-chained ledger that records only actually executed safety steps and gates skips on ledger confirmation, avoiding memory inspection. Across three models and three scenarios, PoEM reduces attack success to 0% with near-zero false positives, minimal overhead, robustness to attacks on itself, and works unchanged in a LangChain agent, while SENTINEL causes 33–50% false positives on legitimate operations.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It reframes agent safety from brittle content heuristics to verifiable execution traces, offering a practical, low-overhead control point that scales with model capability and integrates with common agent stacks.
evaluation.reason: Directly relevant to agentic LLM security: describes FARMA forged-reasoning attack on agent memory and a defenses' limitations (SENTINEL), matching interest in agent attack surfaces and red-teaming/guardrail bypass.

evaluation.title: COMA: A Compositional Misleading Attack Class on Security-RAG, and a Causal Counterfactual Defense
evaluation.summary: The paper defines COMA, a class of compositional misleading attacks on Security-RAG where each retrieved document is true, instruction-free, non-contradictory, and benign, yet their composition misleads the model. They instantiate COMA via action-corruption (correct diagnosis but inferior remediation) and verdict-flip (exploitability destabilized via undecidable reachability), showing consistent success across five models, two synthetic domains, and a real CVE, with verdict-flip degrading but persisting with stronger models; both succeed when the key disambiguating fact must be inferred rather than read. They introduce CCD, a causal counterfactual defense auditing leave-one-out document influence to flag answers dominated by low-trust sources, localize attacker-controlled docs without false positives on benign controls, and catch influence-spreading adversaries via an aggregate variant, releasing attack seeds and a CCD reference implementation.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It tightens the threat model for security-RAG by showing composition-only attacks that evade standard defenses and offers a causal auditing tool that ML security and foundation model researchers can build on or stress-test.
evaluation.reason: Detecting vulnerability signals in model hidden activations speaks to prefill/internal-state monitoring as a defense against code vulnerabilities and new red-teaming/inspection methods.

evaluation.title: Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
evaluation.summary: Auditing step-level credit signals against executed-replay causal ground truth in ALFWorld finds that LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, and policy confidence do not identify causally pivotal steps better than chance, despite performing against annotated correctness. Ground truth contribution is sparse and model-dependent, with substantial variation in counterfactual support across similar-scale policies, and implicit credit tracks policy fluency (high rank correlation) while outcome conditioning adds no causal information. A confidence-only router reduces judge cost modestly without improving pivotal-step detection, and a pre-registered seven-arm training study shows no reliable gains over the base policy, with observed differences attributable to training dose (effective sample size) rather than credit content, implying comparisons must control for dose.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It challenges common step-level credit proxies in agent training and evaluation, highlights the need for causal replay-based auditing, and warns that reported gains may be sample-size artifacts rather than better credit assignment.
evaluation.reason: Direct audit showing step-level credit signals fail to identify causally important agent steps — highly relevant to agent behavior evaluation, red-teaming, and training/credit assignment for tool-using LLM agents.

evaluation.title: MaliciousSkillBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Malicious Agent Skill Detection
evaluation.summary: The authors introduce MaliciousSkillBench, a consolidated benchmark for detecting malicious Agent Skills, normalizing 8,414 raw malicious records into 7,539 unique identities spanning 4,588 structural families and producing a primary set of 9,740 Skills (7,505 malicious, 2,235 benign) after conservative de-duplication and label conflict exclusion. They harmonize 11 attack categories for 4,983 malicious identities and show substantial cross-source threat composition differences. Evaluations of three learned text detectors and three off-the-shelf scanners reveal strong Random/structural-disjoint performance but sharp degradation under Source-Disjoint splits (e.g., TF-IDF SVM 0.932/0.916/0.665 Macro-F1 with 95.6% malicious recall and 62.4% benign FPR on held-out sources), underscoring the need for broader cross-source coverage and joint detection/over-flagging evaluation.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It provides a unified, source-disjoint stress test exposing generalization gaps and FPR trade-offs relevant to LLM agent security and to distribution-shift robustness in foundation models for sequential/structured artifacts.
evaluation.reason: Benchmark consolidating malicious agent Skills addresses a concrete attack surface for agents (malicious skill distribution and detection), directly relevant to LLM security and threat modeling.

evaluation.title: Do All LLMs Know When They're Being Harmful? A Reproducibility Study of Latent-Space Safety Probes Across Model Families
evaluation.summary: This study reproduces Khatri et al.’s pipeline for training lightweight MLP probes on final-layer activations to detect harmful prompts, matching the original LLaMA-3.1-8B results within 0.37 F1 points (0.2 on BeaverTails). It extends the evaluation across Gemma-4-E4B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2-7B on WildJailbreak, BeaverTails, and AEGIS 2.0, finding F1 within about one point of the LLaMA-3.1-8B values using the same probe architecture. It also assesses nondeterminism by varying seeds and reports that final token latent vectors were invariant to seed across architectures.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Suggests simple latent-space probes generalize across model families with stable activations, informing scalable, low-overhead safety detection for LLMs and complementing guardrail strategies.
evaluation.reason: Reproducibility of latent safety probes across model families evaluates a lightweight detection approach that could scale as a defense or monitoring tool for harmful prompt detection.

evaluation.title: Who Verifies the Benchmark? Decentralizing Trust in Large Language Model Evaluation
evaluation.summary: The paper argues that LLM evaluation lacks verifiability and is vulnerable to unverified vendor claims and LLM-judge identity bias, with real-world consequences highlighted by the January 27, 2025 market panic. Using seven verifier models, it measures how disclosing the source model identity shifts scores across 58 factual, reasoning, political, and preference tasks, finding minimal effects on factual items, moderate effects on stress-reasoning, and large effects on geopolitically sensitive topics, with examples including GLM 5.1 (+7.00, p=0.0249) and Llama 3.3 70B (+1.56, p=0.00). It proposes a blockchain-based commit–reveal protocol with Autonomous Economic Agents to create an on-chain, tamper-evident audit trail that separates blind evaluation from post-hoc claims and eases verification for researchers and leaderboard operators.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to LLM security and evaluation: quantifies identity-aware judge bias across sensitive tasks and offers a verifiable, decentralized commit–reveal protocol that could harden benchmark integrity and leaderboards.
evaluation.reason: Model editing for secure code generation evaluates model-level hardening methods versus inference-time approaches — relevant to reducing malicious or vulnerable generations in deployed LLMs.

evaluation.title: RouteGuard: Certifying Routing Gain in LLM Multi-Agent Systems When Complementarity Is Not Enough
evaluation.summary: The paper shows that common assumptions for multi-agent LLM routing—optimizing gate AUC and relying on advisor complementarity—do not determine deployable gain, and introduces RouteGuard to certify routing benefit. It decomposes gain as G = πΔ_E, identifies a conditional-regret functional Φ as the governing quantity (not AUC), provides a finite-sample certification bracket with a matching Le Cam lower bound that is constant-sharp over the fixed-activity class, and observes a robustness phase transition. Experiments on RouterBench and OpenRCA demonstrate RouteGuard acting as a guardrail, certifying gain only under prompt-level sampling (not workload-cluster resampling) on RouterBench and refusing to certify on OpenRCA due to advisor redundancy, with pre-registered semi-synthetic controls confirming calibration thresholds.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It offers a principled, sample-sensitive certification of routing gain that can prevent illusory improvements in LLM multi-agent systems and aligns evaluation with deployment risk.
evaluation.reason: Analyzes routing certification in LLM multi-advisor systems and provides finite-sample guarantees for when routing yields deployable gain—relevant to safe agent composition, evaluation metrics beyond AUC, and deployment-risk assessment.

evaluation.title: Measure, Don't Optimize: Forecasting Recovery in LLM Unlearning
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces J-Access, an inference-time audit that projects intermediate representations into vocabulary space to measure how often target concepts remain accessible along the output pathway, hypothesizing that residual accessibility predicts recovery susceptibility. Auditing 398 public unlearned models across eight methods, they find most retain accessibility above a retain-only gold level, pre-attack accessibility predicts recovery speed and extent at the model level (but not per-fact), and directly minimizing J-Access causes the model to hide knowledge from the audit while increasing post-attack recovery. They conclude J-Access is useful as a model-level diagnostic for residual susceptibility and caution against turning internal audits into optimization targets without validation.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Offers an actionable, model-level risk signal for unlearning robustness and a clear warning about Goodharting internal audits—relevant for designing secure unlearning and audit pipelines in LLMs.
evaluation.reason: Investigates latent recovery after LLM unlearning with an audit (J‑Access) — important for data‑removal/extraction risk monitoring and evaluation methodology.

evaluation.title: TimeSage-EV: A Live Benchmark for Agentic Time Series Analysis in Evolving Environments
evaluation.summary: TimeSage-EV is a live benchmark for agentic time series analysis that evaluates temporal validity and cutoff-aware evidence use across 60 institutional scenarios and 1,485 scenario-period QA pairs from Feb 2023 to May 2026, spanning multiple release cadences. At each period, LLM agents receive time series data and source reports, with withheld target releases serving as ground truth, and are evaluated on state identification, data summarization, and outlook reasoning. Experiments with frontier LLM agents and TimeSage-1.0, a self-evolving agent with a reusable analytical skill library, show substantial performance gaps and recurring failures in temporal validity, exogenous context use, and adaptation, with monthly updates, code, a leaderboard, and failure-mode analyses released.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It offers a continuously updating, real-world benchmark to stress-test LLM agents’ temporal grounding and adaptability—key for secure, cutoff-aware forecasting and decision support in evolving time series contexts.
evaluation.reason: Analysis of when agent skills fail informs robustness and harness design for agentic systems and red-teaming; valuable for understanding failure modes though somewhat broad.

evaluation.title: Stopping and Routing LLM Judge Panels
evaluation.summary: The work frames judge-panel design as a role-conditioned allocation problem that, using a small labeled audit set, declared slices, and judge costs, estimates target-relative roles: copies, complements, and specialists. These roles yield a policy to drop copies, add complements globally, route specialists on slices, and stop when validation gain falls below a threshold, producing a reusable, auditable call plan. It is empirically compared across multiple audit settings against single judges, flat panels, diversity heuristics, full-call stacking, reliability juries, and frugal cascades, yielding a regime map for when to route specialists, stop in saturated regimes, keep broad ensembles, and ignore conditional copies.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete, auditable routing/early-stopping policy for multi-judge LLM evaluation that balances risk and cost across slices—directly relevant to secure deployment and panel design in LLM oversight and verifiers for time-series or reasoning tasks.
evaluation.reason: Optimizing which judges to call and when directly impacts scalable red-teaming, evaluation budgets, and LLM-as-judge pipelines relevant to security and agent verification.

evaluation.title: From Positionwise Confidence to Prefix Scheduling: Verifier Skipping in Speculative Decoding
evaluation.summary: The paper studies verifier skipping in speculative diffusion decoding, introducing a lossy policy that commits selected draft prefixes without invoking the target verifier and asks which confidence signal should schedule skips. It finds that better token predictors do not necessarily yield better schedulers because skipping needs contiguous high-confidence prefixes and short skips can add drafting rounds; it compares raw confidence with learned marginal and conditional survival scores under Strict SDD, lenience, and top-k acceptance baselines. On HumanEval with DiffuCoder-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-32B, all three signals reduce verifier calls by 9.6%–13.5% at the same observed pass@1 as Strict SDD, with raw confidence saving the most despite marginal survival having higher positionwise AUROC, leading to the conclusion that the core challenge is prefix scheduling rather than token prediction alone.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Introduces a new lossy control axis—prefix scheduling for verifier skips—that can cut inference cost in speculative decoding and reveals a counterintuitive gap between positionwise confidence metrics and online efficiency.
evaluation.reason: Speculative decoding verifier-skipping directly impacts LLM inference cost and decoding pipelines; relevant for efficient red-teaming and large-scale automated attacks/agents where verifier invocation is a bottleneck.

evaluation.title: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization where an LLM optimizer iteratively edits a target agent’s harness under expensive, stochastic evaluation with a fixed budget, using only graded feedback and without access to a held-out test partition. A trusted execution environment enforces evaluation boundaries, meters resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit, and performance is measured by normalized gain over the seed harness. Evaluating five frontier LLMs across four tasks and 111 runs, the authors find optimizer models differentiate more than coding harnesses, native harnesses aren’t consistently superior, and gains vary substantially by task and seed regime, establishing harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with room for improvement.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It provides a rigorous, auditable setup to compare LLMs’ agentic self-improvement under realistic noisy/expensive evals—relevant for secure agent orchestration and optimizing time-series/tool-using pipelines.
evaluation.reason: Benchmark for optimizing agent harnesses is directly relevant to LLM agent security (attack surface via prompts/tools/orchestration) and offers an evaluation protocol useful for red-teaming and robust harness design.

evaluation.title: Trident : How to Break Deep Reinforcement Learning Cyber Defenses (Agentic)
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces Trident, an agentic LLM red-teaming framework for evaluating DRL-based cyber defenses, consisting of a dynamic benchmark across CybORG CAGE 4 and CyberWheel, a dataset of 13k+ red-blue trajectories for RLVR, and a Code-as-Policy RLVR architecture. Trident reframes red-agent training as a contextual bandit using a Log Summarizer–Planner–Coder pipeline, where a trainable Planner produces complete attack strategies from compressed logs and a frozen Coder turns them into executable Python policies against live DRL defenders. Empirically, a single 7B planner substantially degrades blue-agent performance (average 522% reduction vs. static red baselines) and uncovers emergent behaviors like decoy avoidance and adaptive state prioritization that static heuristics miss.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It demonstrates an RLVR-driven, code-generating agent that reliably breaks DRL cyber defenses and provides a benchmark/dataset, directly informing LLM security evaluation and agent robustness research.
evaluation.reason: Provides trajectory-level certification methods for modular LLM-based security agents, addressing guarantees and calibration across multi-stage pipelines — useful for safety evaluation of agentic security systems.

evaluation.title: Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies closed-form amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase alignment to retrieved past–future windows before feeding them to a frozen TSFM. On a frozen Chronos-Bolt, it outperforms a state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter across seven benchmark datasets (average −3.75% MSE), and it also improves zero-shot MSE by 2.5%–13.7% on four additional frozen TSFMs without per-backbone tuning. Analysis shows aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts in frozen backbones that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out futures-averaging, suggesting frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It challenges the need for learned fusion in RAG for forecasting by showing closed-form alignment on frozen backbones yields SOTA gains and ridge-like in-context adaptation, a strong baseline relevant to LLM alignment and retrieval studies.
evaluation.reason: DASH improves on-policy self-distillation for reasoning models with temporally-adaptive supervision horizons — relevant to improving RL-style fine-tuning and evaluation of reasoning/judging behavior and scalable red-teaming.

evaluation.title: Tevatron-Elastic: A Unified Abstraction for Training Elastic Retrievers and Rerankers
evaluation.summary: Tevatron-Elastic introduces a unified abstraction that encapsulates three orthogonal elasticity axes for IR models—fewer layers, upper-layer token pruning, and shorter embeddings—so a single checkpoint supports multiple runtime sizes selected via a schedule.
