The abstraction applies uniformly to retrievers and rerankers, encoder and decoder backbones via HF interfaces, subsuming prior methods like Matryoshka embeddings, early exit, 2D Matryoshka (e.g., Starbucks), and layerwise token compression, and also enables Matryoshka LTC for jointly training multiple token-compression ratios in one retriever. Empirically, across 20 checkpoints, three backbones, and two tasks, they report smooth quality curves, near-single-size training cost, and controlled wallclock speedups, releasing the framework and checkpoints for elastic retrieval systems.
evaluation.why_it_matters: A clean, composable interface for multi-axis elasticity in retrievers/rerankers simplifies deployment-time cost/quality trade-offs and unifies techniques ML security and systems folks already use (early exit, Matryoshka, token compression) under one training/checkpoint regime.
evaluation.reason: Elastic retrievers/rerankers address scalable retrieval tradeoffs and dynamic model-size/runtime adaptation—useful for efficient RAG/agent pipelines and evaluation of retrieval components in security workflows.

evaluation.title: ProbGuard: Calibrated Safety Risk Estimation from LLM Output Distributions
evaluation.summary: ProbGuard reframes LLM safety assessment as probabilistic risk estimation over the model’s early output distribution rather than deterministic classification on completed token sequences. It estimates the probability of unsafe continuation via Monte Carlo over generated prefix distributions and calibrates this risk through post-training, enabling early stopping of unsafe generations. Empirically, it achieves the best calibration across nine model–dataset settings (average Brier and ECE reduced by 79.6% and 71.9% vs. the best baseline) and caps jailbreak attack success to ≤1% after only the first ten decoding steps.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It operationalizes distribution-aware, early-stage safety control with strong calibration—useful for red-teaming defenses, risk-sensitive deployment, and aligning with probabilistic guardrail research and time-series-style forecasting over generation trajectories.
evaluation.reason: Proposes a novel metric (feature nonlocality) to assess abstraction level of learned features from sparse autoencoders; useful for mechanistic interpretability and evaluating claims about high-level features relevant to jailbreak/mechanistic work.

evaluation.title: A Four-Axis Trustworthiness Benchmark for LLM-as-Judge in Principle-Based Regulation
evaluation.summary: The paper argues LLM-as-judge for principle-based regulation must be evaluated on four axes: accuracy, paraphrase robustness, adversarial robustness, and calibration, and releases Principle-Bench with 168 FCA-aligned crypto promotion scenarios including paraphrase, keyword-stuffing, and boundary perturbations. It introduces Ceca, a calibrated, auditable assessor emitting per-exemplar counterfactual attributions, and evaluates keyword counting, three sentence-transformer embedders, an open-weight LLM-judge, and a calibrated cascade. Results show no method dominates all axes; a strong 120B judge drops from 0.74 to 0.27 accuracy under keyword-stuffed Consumer Duty inputs and another family’s judge agrees at κ=0.16 on that split, underscoring model-specific failures and the need for per-principle adversarial deception reporting and post-hoc calibration alongside aggregate accuracy.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Offers a concrete, multi-axis benchmark and calibrated assessment method to stress-test LLM judges against paraphrase and adversarial distribution shifts—directly relevant to eval robustness and model governance in safety-critical LLM deployments.
evaluation.reason: LLM-as-judge reliability and adversarial robustness directly relevant to evaluation methodology and guardrail assessment; crypto-financial focus slightly less aligned with core security/time-series interests.

evaluation.title: Probing the Prefill: Detecting Code Vulnerabilities via Latent Activations
evaluation.summary: The authors test whether LLM hidden states during prefill encode vulnerability signals when reading C/C++ code by extracting last prefill token activations from four models and training small MLP probes. Across four function-level benchmarks (Devign, Big-Vul, Draper VDISC, PrimeVul), probes (13.4–16.0M params, <0.2% of base) reach 41.7% average F1, with a Qwen3.5-9B probe hitting 68.8% F1 on Devign, comparable to a fine-tuned-classifier SOTA (67.9%). Performance lags SOTA on the more imbalanced datasets, indicating partial but meaningful vulnerability information in frozen, general-purpose LLM activations and motivating model-native screening approaches.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Shows actionable signal for vulnerability detection resides in prefill activations, suggesting low-overhead, model-native monitors as an alternative or complement to post-hoc judges/classifiers.
evaluation.reason: Reproduction and sensitivity analysis of WEASEL 2.0 across UCR datasets is directly relevant to time-series benchmark validity and practical model choices (ensemble sizing).

evaluation.title: Learning What to Fail On: Failure-Mode Contextual Bandits for Adversarial Data Curation
evaluation.summary: The paper frames adversarial data curation as a failure-mode contextual bandit: RAG generates candidates, the target model filters them, an LLM judge ensemble validates them, and clustering groups recurring failure modes. A stochastic policy samples failure modes for retraining using a validation-based reward that trades off robustness gains, forgetting, and data cost, yielding consistent gains over prior adversarial augmentation on SNLI, ANLI, MultiNLI, and transfer to FEVER with RoBERTa variants. They also provide a theoretical interpretation that failure-mode sampling reduces shortcut-aligned gradient contributions while bounding distributional drift, enabling scalable robustness improvements without human annotation.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It operationalizes adaptive, failure-driven data selection with bandit control and LLM-judged RAG—useful for red-teaming LLMs and for principled, cost-aware adversarial curation relevant to secure training and time-series-style foundation data pipelines.
evaluation.reason: Adversarial data curation via failure-mode contextual bandits targets robustness of NLU models and retrieval-augmented synthetic-data pipelines—highly relevant to scalable red-teaming and adversarial training for LLMs.

evaluation.title: Can a Lightweight Multimodal Model Estimate LLM Reasoning Performance? A Study for Compute-Optimal Document Inference
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces BudgetDoc, a multimodal benchmark with explicit supervision for model-budget-performance trade-offs on three document tasks, addressing the cost and over-thinking issues of uniform inference budgets in LLMs. Using BudgetDoc, the authors train DRB, a ~1B-parameter pre-flight estimator (SigLIP-2 + Qwen3-0.6B) that predicts ordinal model performance across budget levels with a weighted F1 of 0.753. DRB enables dynamic reasoning budget allocation across five frontier models and three datasets, matching or improving F1 over always-maximum-budget baselines in 9/15 settings while reducing cost, and shows preliminary promise for cross-model selection generalization.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It offers a practical path to compute-optimal, layout-aware reasoning allocation and model selection for document tasks, directly relevant to secure and efficient deployment of reasoning LLMs.
evaluation.reason: A lightweight multimodal estimator to predict LLM reasoning performance (compute-budget tradeoffs) is useful for compute-optimal allocation and efficient red-teaming at scale, relevant to security/serving tradeoffs.

evaluation.title: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
evaluation.summary: DreamGuard is a proactive runtime guardrail for LLM agents that uses a risk-aware world model to track a compact recurrent latent state over trajectories and forecast future latent states. From these forecasts, it derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence and fuses multi-horizon signals to decide on interventions before tool executions. Across four benchmarks and an online evaluation, DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive baselines with the best safety-utility trade-off and averages 25 ms end-to-end latency per call.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Introduces a trajectory-aware, low-latency guardrail with explicit risk modeling, aligning with interests in long-horizon safety for LLM agents and bridging to sequence modeling ideas from time series foundation models.
evaluation.reason: Adaptive allocation across model populations for LLM-driven evolutionary search is relevant for cost-efficient red-teaming/evolutionary program search, but more about budgeting than core security.

evaluation.title: SkillTFM: Gated Skill Evolution for Training-Free Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces SkillTFM, a training-free adaptation system for tabular foundation models that replaces parameter updates with gated evolution of agentic skills. It uses a verifiable, extensible skill bank combining boundary evidence identification to characterize task structure and base-model failures with gated skill evolution to retrieve and extend reusable skills under explicit validation. In simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128–0.142, elevating nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898, and shows effectiveness across different TFM backbones.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It proposes a security-adjacent, verifiable skill-gating mechanism for training-free adaptation under distribution shift, echoing modular skill libraries and guarded tool-use in LLMs while targeting tabular/time-series TFMs.
evaluation.reason: Empirical study of self-pretraining for medical time series—useful data on pretraining benefits and transfer in noisy, multimodal TS settings though domain-specific.

evaluation.title: LabelFusion-TS: Fusing Large Language Models, Transformer Encoders, and Financial Time Series for Monetary-Policy Stance Classification
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces LabelFusion-TS, which combines a fine-tuned RoBERTa encoder, a prompted LLM, and an ensemble of time-series transformers over pre-publication market series via a small voting network to classify FOMC sentences as hawkish, dovish, or neutral. Due to limited human labels (~1k sentences), the RoBERTa encoder is first pre-trained on LLM-generated weak labels and then fine-tuned on human annotations. Trained on data up to 2015 and evaluated on 2015–2022, the fused system attains 70.2% weighted F1, surpassing a zero-shot LLM at 64.1% and overtaking it with as few as 240 human-labeled sentences.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It demonstrates measurable gains from fusing market time series with LLM/text encoders for monetary-policy stance classification, highlighting a practical multimodal path beyond text-only classifiers.
evaluation.reason: Multimodal fusion of financial time series with LLMs for stance classification touches the reader's TSFM interest (benchmarks/architectures) and evaluation, though it's a narrow financial NLP application.

evaluation.title: Analysis of Federated Aggregation under Model Poisoning and Backdoor Attacks: A Reconstructed Cross-Dataset and Cross-Architecture Benchmark
evaluation.summary: This work reconstructs a 500-cell federated aggregation benchmark across five methods, five datasets, five architectures, and four conditions (clean, sign-flipping, Gaussian, BadNets), recovering 454 original runs and 36 repairs/reruns, with 10 SVHN cells covered only by summary provenance. Trimmed Mean has the best clean macro-mean accuracy and lowest mean within-task rank, while Krum shows the top recorded accuracy under sign-flipping and Gaussian, and these rankings persist when restricted to fully logged task pairs. Audits reveal the BadNets metric is actually TTLR (all test inputs triggered) and a FedPARETO pathway where reported predictive summaries may not match the corrupted updates used for aggregation, so results are descriptive within recorded configs rather than universal robustness claims.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Highlights reproducibility gaps, metric mis-specification (TTLR), and aggregation/provenance pitfalls that can confound robustness claims in federated settings relevant to secure FL and poisoning/backdoor evaluation.
evaluation.reason: Cross‑dataset benchmark for federated aggregation under poisoning/backdoors informs robust evaluation and threat models though it's more federated learning than LLM‑specific.

evaluation.title: Into the ORBIT for Time Series: Training Regimes for Foundation Models
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces ORBIT, a training paradigm for TSFMs that explicitly controls pre-training distributions via Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling and Omni-Range Incremental Training. It trains Falcon-2.0, a univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction, under this regime. The authors also propose Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment to align shallow and deep representations, and report strong zero-shot forecasting on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench across diverse domains and frequencies.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It provides a principled, controllable pretraining regime and lightweight representation alignment that could transfer to secure LLM pretraining curricula and to robust TSFM deployment across heterogeneous, imbalanced time-series corpora.
evaluation.reason: Evaluation metric for synthetic limit-order-book time series is relevant for TSFM evaluation and assessing generative-model fidelity, with potential security implications for market-simulation attacks.

evaluation.title: Revisiting WEASEL 2.0: Reproduction, Sensitivity, and an Adaptive Ensemble-Size Rule
evaluation.summary: The paper reproduces WEASEL 2.0 on 114 UCR datasets, matching reported accuracy (mean 0.865, median 0.928; Wilcoxon p = 0.655). It probes sensitivity of four design choices, finding the downstream classifier, lack of feature weighting, and the max window-size rule to be robust, while the fixed max ensemble-size rule is over-provisioned for long series. An adaptive rule based on series length and number of classes cuts peak fit memory and time on fixed-length datasets with essentially no median accuracy change.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Offers a principled, resource-saving ensemble-size heuristic for dictionary TSC that preserves accuracy—useful for scaling long-sequence models and benchmarking efficient TS foundations.
evaluation.reason: Reproduction and sensitivity analysis of a time-series classifier (WEASEL 2.0) is directly relevant to TSFM benchmarking and methodological rigor, but it's a classical classifier rather than a foundation-model pretraining advance.

evaluation.title: Feature Priming in Online Linear Regression: Sparse-Regret Lower Bounds and a Tight Univariate Rate
evaluation.summary: The paper studies feature priming for high-dimensional online linear regression and answers a COLT 2023 question negatively for three Moore–Penrose priming rules, showing sparse-logarithmic regret is impossible under a natural past-data protocol. It identifies nuisance interpolation as the mechanism that underweights the predictive coordinate and proves Ω(min{T, sqrt(d)}) regret via Hadamard-style constructions, even against a zero-loss one-sparse comparator, with variants for prime powers and rule selection. On the positive side, it shows regret controlled by data rank and matches this with a Euclidean-normalized triangular lower bound for powered univariate priming (robust to nonnegative ridge), plus a paired ridge construction covering all three powered rules, and reports diagnostics on frozen LM activations reflecting the same failure mode; multivariate and Pearson frontiers remain open.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Clarifies limits of sparsity-seeking online priming and ties them to concrete interpolation pathologies also observed in LM activations, informing robust feature selection and security-relevant guardrails.
evaluation.reason: JEPA/world-model anti-collapse methods and contrastive inverse dynamics propose pretraining objectives relevant to time-series/world-model representation learning, offering alternatives to Gaussian regularizers though not directly TS forecasting.

evaluation.title: Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Generalizable Vulnerability Detection in IoT Firmware
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces IoTVulBench, a human-verified, contamination-screened benchmark for cross-corpus IoT firmware vulnerability detection, and evaluates five model architectures, two tuning methods, and three curriculum strategies with ensemble, distillation, and robustness analyses. Models trained on IoTVulBench outperform matched single-source datasets (MCC 0.58 vs. 0.44 for PrimeVul and 0.39 for D2A), with staged curriculum learning raising MCC to 0.69 and a diversity-optimized ensemble reaching 0.73, surpassing a static analyzer (0.31) and PrimeVul by large margins while maintaining 86% performance under identifier renaming and showing strong calibration and largely faithful explanations. At a 0.5% FPR, the model missed 21% of vulnerabilities versus 71% for the strongest comparator, indicating domain-matched data and curriculum design—not model scale alone—drive generalization in firmware vulnerability detection.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Provides a contamination-screened, human-verified benchmark and concrete training/curriculum/ensemble recipes that substantially improve cross-corpus generalization—useful for LLM security evaluation and for designing data- and curriculum-centric pipelines beyond scaling.
evaluation.reason: IoT firmware vulnerability detection benchmark is relevant to broader adversarial robustness and benchmark validity but outside core LLM/security or time‑series focus.

evaluation.title: Temporal Leakage in Financial News NLP: A Multi-Architecture Audit with a Regime-Specific M&A Signal
evaluation.summary: The paper audits temporal leakage in financial-news direction prediction across 49,799 articles and 16 model–feature setups (TF-IDF, MiniLM, FinBERT, fine-tuned RoBERTa-large/DeBERTa-v3-large, and Llama-3/Qwen2.5 zero/few-shot and LoRA), finding random splits inflate MCC by 1.1×–6.5×, increasing with capacity and feature richness, and that end-to-end FinBERT fine-tuning further amplifies the gap (size-matched ratio 1.75×). Under near-chronological evaluation, only M&A shows a positive locked-test signal (TF-IDF MCC 0.138 train-only, 0.068 after train∪val refit; 10,000-permutation p < 10^{-3}), which does not transfer to FNSPID 2009–2020 U.S. data, suggesting localization to 2024–2025 European-tilted M&A semantics. Three role labelers indicate acquirer-tagged articles as the signal locus, and the authors argue chronological splits purge stale, predictable components, leaving a small, event-localized, lexically shallow residual and call for mandatory leakage audits in financial NLP benchmarks.

model-releases.title: Pre-Compiled Pipeline Shards for Distributed LLM Inference on Intel AI PC Fleets
model-releases.summary: The work demonstrates pipeline-parallel LLM inference across Intel AI PCs by pre-compiling per-layer shards into OpenVINO graphs, with each node running a shard and passing activations onward. They recover monolithic performance by inserting a beam_idx Gather to trigger OpenVINO’s IndirectKVCache fusion, and further improve throughput via speculative decoding and interleaved multi-user micro-batching. Results: a two-node Llama 3.1 8B INT4 pipeline achieves 1.79x the single-user throughput of the unsplit model for two concurrent users and scales to a four-node deployment serving a 70B model with token-identical outputs to non-speculative decoding; code and scripts are provided.
model-releases.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, reproducible recipe to turn idle consumer AI PCs into a distributed LLM serving pool using pipeline sharding with OpenVINO, including concrete tricks (fusion trigger, speculative decoding, interleaved caching) and measured gains.
model-releases.reason: Distributed pipeline-parallel inference across Intel AI PCs is relevant to efficient serving and edge deployment for LLMs (useful for cheap red-teaming at scale), but not security or TSFM research.

longform.title: LabelFusion-TS: Fusing Large Language Models, Transformer Encoders, and Financial Time Series for Monetary-Policy Stance Classification
longform.summary: The paper introduces LabelFusion-TS, which combines a fine-tuned RoBERTa encoder, a prompted LLM, and an ensemble of time-series transformers over pre-publication market series via a small voting network to classify FOMC sentences as hawkish, dovish, or neutral. Due to limited human labels (~1k sentences), the RoBERTa encoder is first pre-trained on LLM-generated weak labels and then fine-tuned on human annotations. Trained on data up to 2015 and evaluated on 2015–2022, the fused system attains 70.2% weighted F1, surpassing a zero-shot LLM at 64.1% and overtaking it with as few as 240 human-labeled sentences.
longform.why_it_matters: It demonstrates measurable gains from fusing market time series with LLM/text encoders for monetary-policy stance classification, highlighting a practical multimodal path beyond text-only classifiers.
longform.reason: Multimodal fusion of financial time series with LLMs for stance classification touches the reader's TSFM interest (benchmarks/architectures) and evaluation, though it's a narrow financial NLP application.

longform.title: Feature Priming in Online Linear Regression: Sparse-Regret Lower Bounds and a Tight Univariate Rate
longform.summary: The paper studies feature priming for high-dimensional online linear regression and answers a COLT 2023 question negatively for three Moore–Penrose priming rules, showing sparse-logarithmic regret is impossible under a natural past-data protocol. It identifies nuisance interpolation as the mechanism that underweights the predictive coordinate and proves Ω(min{T, sqrt(d)}) regret via Hadamard-style constructions, even against a zero-loss one-sparse comparator, with variants for prime powers and rule selection. On the positive side, it shows regret controlled by data rank and matches this with a Euclidean-normalized triangular lower bound for powered univariate priming (robust to nonnegative ridge), plus a paired ridge construction covering all three powered rules, and reports diagnostics on frozen LM activations reflecting the same failure mode; multivariate and Pearson frontiers remain open.
longform.why_it_matters: Clarifies limits of sparsity-seeking online priming and ties them to concrete interpolation pathologies also observed in LM activations, informing robust feature selection and security-relevant guardrails.

longform.title: Ventor-QTest: Threat-Model-Driven Verification of Vendor-Hosted LLM APIs
longform.summary: The paper formalizes hosted model routing as a stochastic process and introduces Ventor-QTest, a black-box audit requiring no probability outputs, with two components: repeated-request estimating average fidelity loss (AFL) via a null-bias-corrected within-window coarsened-KL, and long-sequence estimating extreme fidelity loss (EFL) from the empirical upper tail of a reference-centered-surprisal statistic. AFL shows strong linear agreement with a logprob-based coarsened-KL comparator across three logprob-capable routing conditions, and 20-run sequence probes across seven route snapshots reveal route-specific EFL variation. AFL/EFL exhibit little association with GPQA-Diamond accuracy, but pronounced EFL aligns with reduced Terminal-Bench pass rates under task exposure, motivating joint reporting when auditing long-horizon agentic tasks; code is open-sourced at the provided link.
longform.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, probability-free audit to quantify both average and tail fidelity degradation in vendor-hosted LLM routing, directly relevant to red-teaming and reliability of long-horizon agentic deployments.
longform.reason: Automated vulnerability detection for AI-generated code touches downstream security risks from LLM outputs, useful but more software-security centric than core LLM attack/defense research.
